# 🦍 The hidden `about:` pages: every page `about:about` does not show you

**Mapped on 8 October 2026, on the Gorilla 157.0 candidate (build 28) for Windows and in its source code. Every
page was opened in a fresh, throwaway copy of the browser with its network cut off, so that any attempt to reach
the internet was recorded and none could get out. The changes described here are in the source; the build that
carries them is being built and checked now. Until it is, every line marked "to be confirmed" says so, and this
page will name the build once it has been checked.**

This page is written twice: once in plain language, once with the details. Each page below has both.

### In plain words

Type `about:about` in the address bar and Gorilla shows a list of its own built-in pages. We went through that
list in [the companion page](ABOUT-PAGES.md). Then the maintainer typed an address that was **not** on the list,
`about:fingerprintingprotection`, and a page opened. The question that followed started this work: *why does a
page exist that the list of pages does not show?*

Think of the directory board in the lobby of an office building. It lists the companies on each floor. It does
not list the boiler room, the lift machinery, the cleaners' cupboard or the fire exits. Those rooms are real,
they have doors, and some of them hold the most important equipment in the building. Firefox works the same
way: each built-in page can carry a mark that tells `about:about` to leave it off the board. The page still
exists, and typing its address still opens it. Where the comparison stops: a building's service rooms are
usually locked, and these pages were not. Anyone who knew the address could open them.

So we mapped every one. The Firefox source code names **84** built-in pages. The Gorilla build we started from
registered **70** of them: **40** on the board and **30** hidden. We opened each hidden page, took its picture,
and read the code behind it: who it serves, what it does, and whether it can talk to anyone.

**What we found.** Most hidden pages are plumbing the browser needs: the page you see when a site cannot be
reached, the page that brings back your tabs after a crash, the blank page every new tab starts as. Others were
there for Mozilla, not for you:

- a measuring page for a Mozilla study that fingerprints your computer (`about:fingerprintingprotection`);
- the control desk and the preview screen of Mozilla's in-browser promotions and messages
  (`about:asrouter`, `about:messagepreview`);
- a redirect to Mozilla's referral programme carrying a code that identifies your profile (`about:referrals`);
- four addresses that crash the browser, a tab, the graphics or every add-on the moment you type them;
- pages for features Gorilla does not have, and second names for pages that already have one.

**What we did.** **16** hidden pages are gone from the browser, and where something fed them, that was cut too.
**14** stay, each for a reason written down. The reason for each page, kept or removed, is below.

**What it costs you:** you can no longer crash a tab on purpose to test the crash screen; and if a page does not
load, Gorilla no longer guesses a `www.` name for you. Nothing else you would use is lost. Each page says what
it costs.

**Why it matters.** A browser is the program you trust with everything you read and type. The company that
makes it is the party best placed to reach into it: through updates, studies, messages, measurements. Gorilla
is built on one rule: every channel that can carry code in or data out is a door, and every door is either
justified or closed. Hidden pages are doors nobody checks, because almost nobody knows they are there. Now you
know where they are, and what was behind each one.

### The details: how the pages were found and checked

- **Four ways a page gets in.** A built-in page can be registered (1) in the C++ redirect tables
  (`docshell/base/nsAboutRedirector.cpp`, `browser/components/about/AboutRedirector.cpp`), (2) in the page lists
  of the matching `components.conf` files, (3) as a component contract `@mozilla.org/network/protocol/about;1?what=<name>`
  anywhere in the tree, and (4) by script at run time (DevTools, the new tab page). `about:about` lists only
  pages registered without the `nsIAboutModule::HIDE_FROM_ABOUTABOUT` flag.
- **The map.** `fieldkit build-harness about-registry` reads all four routes in the Gorilla tree and in pristine
  upstream, adds what a built browser actually registered (read inside the running browser), and prints one
  table with the verdict for each page.
- **The pictures and readings.** `fieldkit build-harness about-pages` opens every registered page in a
  throwaway copy of the browser with a fresh profile and a dead proxy (`127.0.0.1:9`), records its text, the
  pictures it draws, script errors and every request it tries; with `shots=` it saves a picture of each page
  drawn by the browser itself. Error pages are empty when opened by their address, so the probe `error-pages`
  produces each one by its real cause on this machine: a refused connection, a port the browser refuses, a
  self-signed certificate, an `about:` address nothing registers, and a plain-HTTP site under HTTPS-Only (on a
  made-up name resolved locally: HTTPS-Only never upgrades an address that points back at this computer).
- **The source reading.** Each hidden page was traced in the code: its registration and flags, what opens it,
  what it can contact, and what depends on it. The notes are kept with the maintainer's harness.
- **The register.** Every one of the 84 names has a verdict, keep or remove, with its reason, in the
  maintainer's register (decision D-157-40). It is enforced twice: **before** every build (a page the source
  can register that the register does not know, or a removed page that came back, stops the build) and
  **after** it (the pages the built browser registers must match the register). When Firefox adds a new hidden
  page, the build stops until someone reviews it, and this document fails its own check until the page is
  explained here.

## Removed

<a id="about-fingerprintingprotection"></a>

### `about:fingerprintingprotection`: The hidden page that measured your computer

![about:fingerprintingprotection](screenshots/hidden-pages/about-fingerprintingprotection.png)

**Removed (D-157-40).** **Talks to:** none from the page; it fed Mozilla's user-characteristics ping

#### In plain words

**What it is.** about:fingerprintingprotection was a measuring page. It worked like the measuring room of a clinic that runs a research study: a nurse records your height, reach, eyesight and hearing, not to treat you, but so that researchers can learn how much people differ from one another. This page did the same to your computer, for a study Mozilla calls "user-characteristics". It measured how this copy of the browser draws pictures, which fonts and voices it has, what its screen, processor and keyboard are, and much more, so that Mozilla's researchers could tune Firefox's protection against fingerprinting. Where the comparison stops: you walk into a clinic's measuring room knowingly, and you see the nurse. This page was opened by the browser itself, in a browser window that is never drawn on the screen, and nothing told you it had run.

Fingerprinting means recognising a browser by describing it, with no cookie needed: its screen, its fonts, the exact way it draws a shape, its time zone. To learn how to protect people from being recognised this way, Mozilla's study collected those same details from its own users.

**When you would meet it.** Never, unless you typed its address. You would not have found it by looking: about:about, the browser's own list of its built-in pages, did not show it. That is how this page started the whole audit. The maintainer came across it while customising Gorilla's pages and asked why about:about did not list it.

The answer is a flag in the source code called `HIDE_FROM_ABOUTABOUT`. Think of the directory board in the lobby of an office building: it lists the offices and leaves out the boiler room, the cleaning cupboard and the post room. The flag puts a page among the service rooms. Where the comparison stops: in a real building the service rooms are usually locked, and a hidden page is not locked at all. Anyone who types its exact address walks straight in. The flag takes the name off the board and does nothing else.

That question led us to every page the source can register. The source names 84 about: pages; the build registered 70; about:about listed 40 and hid 30. We opened and pictured every hidden page and read each one in the source, and 16 pages were removed. This document is the result.

The browser opened this page out of sight. During start-up, once three things had happened (the start-up work was finished, the graphics system was ready and the list of fonts was ready), the browser checked whether a measurement was due. If it was, it loaded this page in an invisible browser and measured. A measurement was due once per "wave" of the study: each time Mozilla raised the study's version number above the last one this copy had sent. A person could also force one collection by hand, with a setting named `toolkit.telemetry.user_characteristics_ping.send-once`.

**What you see.** The picture was taken on the Gorilla build that still had the page, opened by typing its address. At the top is the heading "Test Canvases", then "WebGL Canvas" and a black square holding a tilted square whose corners shade from white to red, green and blue. Under it is an empty box labelled "ImageData:". Then comes "Test Canvases Software" and the same drawing again. Further down, out of the picture, the page draws about 30 mathematical formulas. There are no buttons and nothing to choose.

The drawings are not decoration. The same shape is drawn once with the graphics card and once without it, because the tiny differences in how two computers draw the same picture are part of a fingerprint. A fingerprint works like describing a stranger by height, accent, coat and walk: no single detail names them, but together the details often pick one person out of a crowd. Where the comparison stops: a person can change coat in a minute, while a computer cannot change its graphics card or its fonts on a whim, so the description stays useful for a long time.

Opened by hand, the page worked out all its measurements and gave them to nobody, because the part of the browser that receives them only exists while a real collection is running.

A collection measured, as listed in the source:

- Graphics: drawings made with and without the graphics card (WebGL versions 1 and 2), flat drawings and drawn text, the newer WebGPU graphics system, and the exact sizes of drawn shapes, emoji and text.
- Sound and speech: the voices the computer can speak with, which audio and video formats it can play, an "audio fingerprint" (how the computer processes a test sound), the properties of its audio devices, and the audio and video devices attached.
- Screen and input: screen and window details, zoom, pointer and touch abilities, game controllers, motion sensors.
- Text: installed and missing fonts, font settings, how text is smoothed and drawn, how mathematical formulas are laid out, the system colours and the display preferences that pages can ask about.
- The machine: how many processors it reports, the processor model, the keyboard layout, the languages, the time zone, how much storage the browser may use, security-key (WebAuthn) abilities, the browser's identification string, the exact results of some mathematical calculations, which media features are switched off, and a selection of other settings.
- Network: the page asked the browser's video-call system (WebRTC) to list this computer's own network connection points, and the list of formats it supports for calls. No outside server was involved, so only local addresses were gathered.

Not all the measuring happened inside the invisible page. While a collection ran, the browser registered two helpers that were allowed into ordinary web tabs, and it took the window and screen details and the flat drawings inside the tabs you had open.

**Does it talk to anyone?** The page itself contacts no one. Its security rules let it load only the browser's own files, and its network test used no outside server. Its job was to fill in a report, the "user-characteristics" ping, which the browser would send to Mozilla. The report left out the identifier that ordinary telemetry uses, but it carried one of its own: a random code stored in your profile (the folder where the browser keeps your settings). It was meant to travel through OHTTP, a relay designed to hide which computer sent it. Picture a letter sent through a forwarding service that removes the return address. Where the comparison stops: the relay hides where the letter came from, not what it says, and here the letter is a detailed description of the computer, signed with the same made-up name every time, so letters from one computer can still be matched to each other.

In Gorilla the report could not leave, even before our change, for two separate reasons.

1. The wave never came. The version number that starts a wave begins at 0, and only Nimbus, Mozilla's system for running experiments on users from a distance, ever raises it. Gorilla enrols no one in Nimbus: its experiment checks all answer no, and its experiment loader is locked off.
2. The post box is bricked up. If a person forced a collection with the send-once setting, the full measurement would have run on their computer, but the finished report goes to Glean, Mozilla's data-collection library. Gorilla never starts Glean, and its upload switch is locked off. Nothing would have left the machine.

**What we did, and why.** Removed, and the collection that used it can no longer start. The browser no longer registers the page, so the address no longer opens anything. There was a second way in: Firefox lets you open a page's own file directly by its internal address, one that starts with chrome://. The page's files are no longer packed into the browser, so that way is closed too. The start-up check that launched a collection is cut out of the source. The study's opt-out setting is locked on, and the send-once setting is locked off. The rest of the measuring code is still in the source, but nothing in a normal run of the browser can reach it.

Why remove something that could not send anything? Because a door that is closed only by a setting is still a door. A setting is a latch, not a wall: whoever can change settings can open it, whether that is you, an add-on, a company policy, a future update, or a remote-configuration system such as Nimbus, which existed to raise exactly this number. We design against the company that ships a browser and anyone who can lean on that company, and we close every channel that can carry data out unless it earns its place. This one served Mozilla's researchers, not the person at the keyboard. A hidden page is a door nobody checks.

Two more reasons. First, the browser gave this address special treatment by name: a page loaded at it could play sound without a click, receive motion-sensor readings while in the background, and use drawing features that ordinary web pages are refused. A name that carries privileges is worth keeping only if something you need uses it. Second, removing the page alone would have left a trap: had anyone forced a collection afterwards, the invisible browser would have waited for ever for a page that no longer exists. So the start of the collection is cut as well.

**What it costs you.** Nothing you would notice. You lose the chance to give your computer's measurements to Mozilla's fingerprinting research, which in Gorilla could never be sent anyway.

**The lesson.** Protection research and tracking can use the same measurements. To learn how browsers can be recognised, this study measured the very details a tracker would use. That does not make it sinister, but it does make it a channel. The useful question about any browser is not "does it collect?" but "what decides whether it sends, and who can change that?" Here the answer was a handful of settings and a number that only a remote system could raise. Hidden from the list did not mean locked; it meant unchecked.

#### For developers

Line numbers are those of the source before the D-157-40 change.

**Registration**

- `docshell/base/nsAboutRedirector.cpp:124-129`, listed in `docshell/build/components.conf:16`. The page is `usercharacteristics.html` with its script `usercharacteristics.js` (resistfingerprinting `jar.mn:7-12`).
- Flags (upstream): `URI_SAFE_FOR_UNTRUSTED_CONTENT | HIDE_FROM_ABOUTABOUT | ALLOW_SCRIPT | URI_MUST_LOAD_IN_CHILD | URI_CAN_LOAD_IN_PRIVILEGEDABOUT_PROCESS`. It loads in the privileged about content process; the collection's `UserCharacteristics` window actor is registered for remote type `privilegedabout` only.
- `HIDE_FROM_ABOUTABOUT` only drops the entry from about:about's list. It does not restrict loading: typing the address opened the page (see the picture).

**What opened it**

1. `toolkit/components/resistfingerprinting/nsRFPService.cpp:466-479`: fires once three observer topics have been seen (idle start-up tasks done, compositor created, font list initialised).
2. `nsUserCharacteristics::MaybeSubmitPing` (`nsUserCharacteristics.cpp:1455-1464`), gated by `ShouldSubmit`.
3. `PopulateDataAndEventuallySubmit` (lines 1467-1536), then `ContentPageStuff` (lines 159-197).
4. `createContentPage` in `UserCharacteristicsPageService.sys.mjs:80-146` loads the page in a hidden browser (`HiddenBrowserManager.withHiddenBrowser`) and awaits the page's data event.

**The gate (`ShouldSubmit`, `nsUserCharacteristics.cpp:1379-1452`)**

- `toolkit.telemetry.user_characteristics_ping.opt-out` wins over everything (line 1390).
- Resist Fingerprinting on, or any fingerprinting-protection overrides set, blocks it (lines 1394-1416).
- `toolkit.telemetry.user_characteristics_ping.send-once` forces it (line 1418). Upstream it is not locked (`modules/libpref/init/all.js:597`).
- Otherwise `current_version` must exceed `last_version_sent`. `current_version` defaults to 0 (`all.js:589`); only the Nimbus feature `userCharacteristics` raises it (`FeatureManifest.yaml:4226-4236`). One "wave" is one raise.

**What it measured**

- Page script (`usercharacteristics.js:1641-1661`): WebGL renders (hardware and forced-software); speech voices, media codec capabilities, an audio fingerprint, audio device properties; pointer and touch; WebRTC ICE host-candidate foundations and the SDP codec list; WebAuthn capabilities, storage quota, motion sensors; MathML layout, CSS media queries, system colours, system fonts; element rectangles and SVG/emoji text sizes; navigator properties and time zone.
- Service (`UserCharacteristicsPageService.sys.mjs:160-180`): locale and zoom, disabled media prefs, Math function results; gamepads, client and CPU information; screen, pointer and window information; WebGL parameters (versions 1 and 2, hardware and software); 2D canvas and font renders, WebGPU, user agent.
- C++ (`nsUserCharacteristics.cpp:1488-1513`): media devices, time zone; fingerprinted and missing fonts, font prefs, anti-aliasing, smoothing and rendering settings, math font; CSS and system preferences, screen, selected prefs; keyboard layout, languages; processor count, CPU model, miscellaneous.
- The page offers no actions: two canvases and about 30 MathML formulas.

**Network**

- Page CSP: resource: and chrome: only (`usercharacteristics.html:9-12`).
- WebRTC: `media.peerconnection.default_iceservers` is `"[]"` (`all.js:305`): no STUN or TURN, host candidates only.
- Ping `user-characteristics` (`toolkit/components/resistfingerprinting/pings.yaml:8-16`): no telemetry client ID, but its own UUID pref (`nsUserCharacteristics.cpp:1341-1354`); uploaded through OHTTP. Submitted at lines 1539-1543.
- Why nothing could leave Gorilla even before D-157-40: `FOG::InitializeFOG` returns before doing anything (`toolkit/components/glean/xpcom/FOG.cpp:155-158`); `datareporting.healthreport.uploadEnabled` is false and locked (`browser/app/profile/firefox.js:3925`); Nimbus studies, rollouts and Labs all return false (`toolkit/components/nimbus/ExperimentAPI.sys.mjs:469-479`) and the Remote Settings experiment loader is locked off (`firefox.js:4067`). With `send-once` set by hand, the whole collection still ran locally and the submit call went into a Glean that was never started.

**Surprising**

- The address is privileged by name. `nsContentUtils.cpp:1241-1248` creates an about:fingerprintingprotection principal; documents with it get autoplay without a click (`AutoplayPolicy.cpp:121-125`), motion-sensor events while in the background (`nsDeviceSensors.cpp:213-217`) and chrome-only WebIDL (`CanvasRenderingContext2D.webidl:39, 79`; `WebGLRenderingContext.webidl:55`; `WebGPU.webidl:131`; gate at `nsRFPService.cpp:2618-2632`).
- During a collection two window actors (`UserCharacteristicsWindowInfo`, `UserCharacteristicsCanvasRendering`) are registered with no address filter and `safeForUntrustedWebProcess: true` (`UserCharacteristicsPageService.sys.mjs:316-329, 687-697`). Window and screen information and the 2D canvas renders are taken inside the user's open web tabs.
- Opened by hand, the page computes everything and the result goes nowhere: the receiving actor is registered only during a collection (`UserCharacteristicsPageService.sys.mjs:84-98`).
- Removing only the about: entry would leave a hang: with `send-once` set, the hidden browser waits for ever for data from a page that cannot load (`UserCharacteristicsPageService.sys.mjs:100-131`).

**What Gorilla changed (D-157-40)**

- The entry is gone from `docshell/base/nsAboutRedirector.cpp` and `docshell/build/components.conf`; the address no longer opens anything.
- `toolkit/components/resistfingerprinting/jar.mn`: the six usercharacteristics files (`usercharacteristics.html`, `usercharacteristics.js`, `usercharacteristics.css`, `usercharacteristics.woff`, `gl-matrix.js`, `ssdeep.js`) are not packaged. In Firefox a page file's chrome:// address opens directly from the address bar, a second way into a page whose about: entry is gone; for this page that way is closed too.
- `toolkit/components/resistfingerprinting/nsRFPService.cpp`: the start-up hook no longer calls `nsUserCharacteristics::MaybeSubmitPing()` (marker comment `GORILLA D-157-40 (2026-10-08): no user-characteristics collection.`).
- `modules/libpref/init/all.js`: `toolkit.telemetry.user_characteristics_ping.opt-out` is true and locked; `toolkit.telemetry.user_characteristics_ping.send-once` is false and locked.
- Left in the source, unreachable: `nsUserCharacteristics.cpp`, `UserCharacteristicsPageService.sys.mjs`, the actors, the metrics, the ping definition and the Nimbus feature entry. No normal start-up path reaches them. The one remaining caller is the test observer topic `user-characteristics-testing-please-populate-data`, which `nsRFPService.cpp` honours only when `xpc::IsInAutomation()` is true.

<a id="about-asrouter"></a>

### `about:asrouter`: Mozilla's in-browser messaging control desk

![about:asrouter](screenshots/hidden-pages/about-asrouter.png)

**Removed (D-157-40).** **Talks to:** on click (Mozilla's Remote Settings and documentation; message images from Mozilla's CDN)

#### In plain words

**What it is.** about:asrouter was the control desk of Mozilla's messaging system inside the browser. That system, called ASRouter, decides which messages the browser shows you: the "recommended feature" pop-ups, the large "spotlight" windows in the middle of the screen, information bars across the window, speech-bubble tours that point at a button, badges on toolbar buttons, system notifications, promotions in private windows, and the welcome pages for new users. The page worked like the control desk behind a department store's announcements and in-store posters: staff choose which announcement plays and which poster goes where, can play any announcement at once to test it, can see the rules that decide which customers hear what, and can reset the count of how often each customer has heard each one. Where the comparison stops: in a shop, the announcements belong to the shop you chose to walk into; here the shop floor is your own computer, the announcer is the company that made the browser, and the desk sat inside your copy of the browser.

**When you would meet it.** Never, unless you typed its address. The browser never opens it. The only link to it was on another page for developers, the admin page of the Discovery Stream feed on the new tab page.

**What you see.** The picture was taken on the Gorilla build that still had the page. The tab is titled "ASRouter Admin". The page shows a single line and nothing else: it tells you to set the preference `browser.newtabpage.activity-stream.asrouter.devtoolsEnabled` to true and reload the page. That preference was the page's switch, and it was off. With the switch on, the page became a full console. It could:

- list every message and every message source, and block or unblock any message;
- force any message onto the screen, including one whose text had been edited by hand;
- copy a message as a link to about:messagepreview (described next in this document);
- turn message sources on or off by rewriting their settings;
- test the targeting rules (the conditions that decide who sees a message) and show every fact those rules can read;
- reset or edit the record of how many times you have seen each message;
- force the browser's "install attribution", the note of where its download came from, by writing the file that holds it on Windows.

Turning the switch on also added a set of test messages.

**Does it talk to anyone?** The page fetched nothing by itself. It held links you could click: to firefox.settings.services.mozilla.com, Mozilla's Remote Settings service, which sends data to browsers, and to Mozilla's documentation for developers. Pressing "Show" on one of the built-in messages could load its pictures from firefox-settings-attachments.cdn.mozilla.net, Mozilla's file server; the spotlight window's security rules allow that address.

In Firefox, messages come from three places: Remote Settings (Mozilla's servers), Nimbus (Mozilla's experiment system) and a set of welcome messages built into the browser. In Gorilla only the built-in messages can exist. Remote Settings never contacts a server and carries no packaged copy of these message lists; the loader that would fetch messages from a plain web address is disabled; and Nimbus enrols no one. The messaging system itself still starts every time the browser starts. It is the console that is gone.

**What we did, and why.** Removed. The browser no longer registers the page, so the address no longer opens anything. Its files are no longer packed into the browser either, so its internal chrome:// address, a second way in, does not open it. Its switch is locked off, so it cannot be turned on from about:config. The same switch also brought the message preview page's helper to life and added the test messages, so those stay off too.

The console's commands are now refused whoever sends them. That matters because the console was never the only page that could send them. The part of the browser that carries them out never checked which page a command came from, so the welcome page (about:welcome), the new tab page (about:newtab), the home page (about:home) and the private-window page (about:privatebrowsing) could send the same commands: force or edit a message, unblock every message, switch message sources on and off, force the install attribution. Now each of those commands is refused unless the console's switch is on, and the switch is locked off.

The messaging system is a channel from Mozilla to your screen. It decides what to show you, when, and on the strength of what it knows about your browser. Gorilla already keeps Mozilla's servers out of it. The console served Mozilla's messaging and marketing staff and its developers, never the person using the browser, and with its switch on it could force messages, rewrite settings and write a file to your disk. We design against the company that ships the browser and anyone who can lean on it, so a control desk for a channel aimed at you has no place here.

**What it costs you.** Nothing you would notice. You lose a tool for testing Mozilla's messages, which only the people who write those messages use.

**The lesson.** The "did you know?" pop-ups in a browser are not random tips. They come from a rule engine with its own console, its own message sources and its own record of what you have already seen, and the rules choose who sees what from facts about the browser. Once you know that machinery exists, you can ask where its messages come from. We asked: in Gorilla, only the messages built into the browser are left.

#### For developers

Line numbers are those of the source before the D-157-40 change.

**Registration**

- `browser/components/about/AboutRedirector.cpp:51-55`, listed in `browser/components/about/components.conf:8`. The page is `browser/components/asrouter/content/asrouter-admin.html`, a React page built from `content-src/components/ASRouterAdmin/ASRouterAdmin.jsx`.
- Flags (upstream): `URI_SAFE_FOR_UNTRUSTED_CONTENT | URI_CAN_LOAD_IN_PRIVILEGEDABOUT_PROCESS | URI_MUST_LOAD_IN_CHILD | ALLOW_SCRIPT | HIDE_FROM_ABOUTABOUT`: privileged about content process, not listed in about:about.
- Nothing in the browser opens it. The only link is "Click here" in the new tab Discovery Stream admin page (`browser/extensions/newtab/content-src/components/DiscoveryStreamAdmin/DiscoveryStreamAdmin.jsx:1384`).

**Behaviour**

- Unless `browser.newtabpage.activity-stream.asrouter.devtoolsEnabled` is true the page renders only "You must enable…" (`ASRouterAdmin.jsx:1577-1588`). Default false (`ASRouterPreferences.sys.mjs:242-249`).
- With the pref on: list messages and providers, block and unblock; force-show any message, including edited JSON (`ASRouterParentProcessMessageHandler.sys.mjs:133-138`); copy a message as an about:messagepreview link (`ASRouterAdmin.jsx:582-593`); switch providers by rewriting their prefs (`ASRouterPreferences.sys.mjs:145-168`); evaluate targeting expressions and show all targeting parameters; reset or edit impression counts (`ASRouter.sys.mjs:2427`); force install attribution, which writes the Windows attribution file (`ASRouter.sys.mjs:2520-2542`).
- The pref also adds the PanelTestProvider test messages (`ASRouterPreferences.sys.mjs:76-83, 132-138`).
- ASRouter itself starts on every launch (`browser/components/BrowserGlue.sys.mjs:1238-1240`) and carries on without the page.

**Message sources and network**

- Upstream providers (`browser/app/profile/firefox.js:2039-2042`): `cfr` and `message-groups` (Remote Settings collections), `onboarding` (local), `messaging-experiments` (Nimbus).
- In this tree only the local messages can exist: the plain URL loader is stubbed (`ASRouter.sys.mjs:226-230`); Remote Settings has a dummy server URL and skips every remote action (`services/settings/Utils.sys.mjs:107-125`, sync guard `RemoteSettingsClient.sys.mjs:653-657`), loads only packaged dumps (`Utils.sys.mjs:146-156`) and has no dump for `cfr`, `message-groups` or `ms-language-packs` (`services/settings/dumps/main/moz.build`); Nimbus has no enrolments.
- The page fetches nothing automatically. The old preview endpoint is already dead upstream (`asrouter-utils.mjs:104-106`).
- On click: links to firefox.settings.services.mozilla.com (`ASRouterAdmin.jsx:956, 971`) and to the developer docs (`ASRouterAdmin.jsx:1650`). "Show" on a local message can load images from firefox-settings-attachments.cdn.mozilla.net (for example `OnboardingMessageProvider.sys.mjs:554`), which the spotlight CSP allows (`browser/base/content/spotlight.html:11`).

**Surprising**

- Upstream, the parent process does not check which page sends the admin messages: about:welcome, about:newtab, about:home and about:privatebrowsing can send them too (`DesktopActorRegistry.sys.mjs:804-810`; `ASRouterChild.sys.mjs:90-112`). Only editing impression state checks the devtools pref (`ASRouter.sys.mjs:2428`). Removing the page alone would not shrink this surface; Gorilla now refuses the commands themselves (below).
- Forcing attribution sets the test-only environment variable `XPCSHELL_TEST_PROFILE_DIR` inside a normal browser process (`ASRouter.sys.mjs:2535`).

**What Gorilla changed (D-157-40)**

- The entry is gone from `browser/components/about/AboutRedirector.cpp` and `browser/components/about/components.conf`; the address no longer opens anything.
- `browser/components/asrouter/jar.mn`: `asrouter-admin.html`, `asrouter-admin.bundle.js` and `ASRouterAdmin.css` (`jar.mn:9-11` before the change) are not packaged, so the page's chrome:// address does not open either.
- `browser/app/profile/firefox.js`: `browser.newtabpage.activity-stream.asrouter.devtoolsEnabled` is false and locked. That also keeps the PanelTestProvider messages out.
- `browser/components/asrouter/modules/ASRouterParentProcessMessageHandler.sys.mjs`: a `CONSOLE_COMMANDS` set holds the console's commands (`ADMIN_CONNECT_STATE`, `UNBLOCK_MESSAGE_BY_ID`, `UNBLOCK_ALL`, `BLOCK_BUNDLE`, `UNBLOCK_BUNDLE`, `DISABLE_PROVIDER`, `ENABLE_PROVIDER`, `EVALUATE_JEXL_EXPRESSION`, `EXPIRE_QUERY_CACHE`, `FORCE_ATTRIBUTION`, `FORCE_PRIVATE_BROWSING_WINDOW`, `OVERRIDE_MESSAGE`, `MODIFY_MESSAGE_JSON`, `RESET_PROVIDER_PREF`, `SET_PROVIDER_USER_PREF`, `RESET_GROUPS_STATE`, `RESET_MESSAGE_STATE`, `RESET_SCREEN_IMPRESSIONS`, `EDIT_STATE`). `handleMessage` rejects any of them unless `devtoolsEnabled` is true, and that pref is locked false. The commands are refused whoever sends them, which closes the about:welcome, about:newtab, about:home and about:privatebrowsing path described above.
- Left in place: the `about:asrouter` entries in `DesktopActorRegistry.sys.mjs` (lines 512 and 805) and the Discovery Stream link, which now points at an address that opens nothing.

<a id="about-messagepreview"></a>

### `about:messagepreview`: The preview stage for Mozilla's messages

![about:messagepreview](screenshots/hidden-pages/about-messagepreview.png)

**Removed (D-157-40).** **Talks to:** conditional (message images from Mozilla's CDN; message buttons run privileged actions)

#### In plain words

**What it is.** about:messagepreview showed one message from Mozilla's messaging system (the about:asrouter entry explains that system) on the real part of the browser where it would appear: a spotlight window, an information bar, a recommendation pop-up and so on. The whole message travelled inside the page's address, written in a coded form after `?json=`. It worked like a theatre's dress rehearsal: you hand the stage manager a script and the scene is played on the real stage with the real props, so you see exactly what the audience will see. Where the comparison stops: stage props are harmless, while here the props were real buttons, and pressing one did the real thing: open a web address, install an add-on from a web address, or change a browser setting.

**When you would meet it.** Never, unless you typed its address or opened a link to it. The browser never opens it. The only links to it were made by the Share button of about:asrouter. It served Mozilla's messaging and marketing staff, developers, and an add-on called nimbus-devtools that is not part of Gorilla.

**What you see.** The picture was taken on the Gorilla build that still had the page, opened with no message. It shows a large grey drawing of a light bulb with a leaf on top and short strokes around it like rays, and in the top-left corner a small drawing of a light switch. The tab carries a light-bulb icon. Nothing else happens. The page's helper only existed while the messaging console's switch, `browser.newtabpage.activity-stream.asrouter.devtoolsEnabled`, was on; with the switch off, as here, the page was an empty shell whose functions did nothing.

With the switch on, a link carrying a message put that message on screen. The page could show information bars, spotlight windows, recommendation pop-ups, the private-window new tab promotion, the sidebar chatbot promotion, speech-bubble feature tours and a button on the bookmarks toolbar. Two of these changed your browser on the way: the feature tour first cleared the record of which tours you had seen, and the bookmarks-toolbar message made the bookmarks toolbar visible. The light switch in the corner swapped the browser to its built-in compact dark or compact light theme, to show the message both ways. It did so by switching the real theme add-on, a lasting change rather than a preview; the page put your previous theme back when it closed. The browser also checked each message against a description of what a valid message looks like, and showed it even when the check failed, noting the error only in a log.

**Does it talk to anyone?** The page itself fetched nothing: its security rules allowed only the browser's own files. With the switch on, a message it showed could load pictures from Mozilla's file server, firefox-settings-attachments.cdn.mozilla.net, which the spotlight window's security rules allow. And a message's buttons ran their actions when clicked: opening a web address, installing an add-on from a web address, or setting a preference.

**What we did, and why.** Removed. The browser no longer registers the page, so the address no longer opens anything. Its whole folder is no longer built, so the page's files are not in the browser at all, and its internal chrome:// address, a second way in, does not open it either. Its helper has been taken out of the browser's list of helpers, and the switch that brought the helper to life is locked off.

The danger was in the design. Once the switch was on, anyone who could get you to open a link could stage a message on your screen, inside the browser's own windows, with buttons that carry privileged actions. A message dressed as the browser itself carries the browser's authority. That is a door aimed straight at you, and it served Mozilla's marketing work, not you.

**What it costs you.** Nothing you would notice, unless you write messages for Mozilla's messaging system and want to see them on screen.

**The lesson.** In a browser, an address is not always a place; it can be an instruction. This one carried a whole message, buttons included, and the browser's own windows displayed it. Whenever an address can make the browser do something rather than show something, ask who is able to send you that address.

#### For developers

Line numbers are those of the source before the D-157-40 change.

**Registration**

- `browser/components/about/AboutRedirector.cpp:89-94`, listed in `browser/components/about/components.conf:17`. The page is `messagepreview.html` with `messagepreview.js`, built from `browser/components/messagepreview/` (`browser/components/moz.build:48`).
- Flags (upstream): `URI_MUST_LOAD_IN_CHILD | URI_CAN_LOAD_IN_PRIVILEGEDABOUT_PROCESS | URI_SAFE_FOR_UNTRUSTED_CONTENT | ALLOW_SCRIPT | HIDE_FROM_ABOUTABOUT`.
- The `AboutMessagePreview` actor is registered only when `browser.newtabpage.activity-stream.asrouter.devtoolsEnabled` is true (`DesktopActorRegistry.sys.mjs:133-146`, specifically 144-145). With default prefs the page is an empty div whose functions are undefined.
- Nothing in the browser opens it. The only links come from the admin page's Share button (`ASRouterAdmin.jsx:512, 582-593`). The external nimbus-devtools add-on also uses it (`AboutMessagePreviewParent.sys.mjs:140`).

**Behaviour**

- `messagepreview.js:21-46` decodes Base64 JSON from `?json=`. The child calls the show function only if the devtools pref is on (`AboutMessagePreviewChild.sys.mjs:41-46`).
- The parent checks the message against a local schema, logs a failure and shows the message anyway (`AboutMessagePreviewParent.sys.mjs:181-192`).
- Message types handled (`AboutMessagePreviewParent.sys.mjs:63-130`): infobar, spotlight, CFR doorhanger, private-window newtab, sidebar chatbot promo; feature callout, which first clears tour prefs (lines 80-83); bookmarks-bar button, which forces the bookmarks toolbar visible.
- The light switch turns on the built-in compact dark or light theme (lines 218-223); when the page closes it re-enables the previous theme (lines 147-160). It is a lasting add-on change, not a preview.

**Network**

- Automatic: none from the page. Its CSP allows only chrome: and resource: (`messagepreview.html:11-14`).
- Conditional: with the pref on, a shown message can pull images from firefox-settings-attachments.cdn.mozilla.net (spotlight CSP).
- On click: buttons run built-in message actions such as opening a URL, installing an add-on from a URL or setting a pref (`SpecialMessageActions.sys.mjs:870, 928, 1102`).

**Surprising**

- Once the pref is on, a pasted link from anyone can stage a message whose buttons carry privileged actions.

**What Gorilla changed (D-157-40)**

- The entry is gone from `browser/components/about/AboutRedirector.cpp` and `browser/components/about/components.conf`; the address no longer opens anything.
- `browser/components/moz.build`: the `messagepreview` directory (line 48 before the change) is no longer built, so `messagepreview.html`, `messagepreview.js` and both actors are not in the browser; the page's chrome:// address does not open either.
- `DesktopActorRegistry.sys.mjs`: the `AboutMessagePreview` actor entry (lines 133-146 before the change) is gone.
- The pref that gated the actor is false and locked in `browser/app/profile/firefox.js`.

<a id="about-referrals"></a>

### `about:referrals`: The forwarding address for Firefox referrals

![about:referrals](screenshots/hidden-pages/about-referrals.png)

**Removed (D-157-40).** **Talks to:** conditional (www.firefox.com/invite with a per-profile referral code)

#### In plain words

**What it is.** about:referrals was a forwarding address. When it worked, it sent you on to Mozilla's "Share Firefox" invitation page, https://www.firefox.com/invite/, with a referral code added to the address. The code is made once for your profile (the folder where the browser keeps your settings, bookmarks and history): 16 random characters, stored in a setting named `browser.referrals.code` and then locked so that it cannot be changed. It worked like the "refer a friend" card from a gym or a phone shop, printed with your own member number, so that the shop knows who sent each new customer. Where the comparison stops: you decide where a printed card goes, while here the code went to Mozilla's website the moment you opened the share page, and it was the same code every time, so the website could tell that every visit came from the same profile. A code that never changes and travels with you is what this document calls a lasting identifier.

**When you would meet it.** Never in Gorilla. In Firefox the ways in are a button in the main menu, an item in the Help menu (and in the application menu on a Mac), a "Share Firefox" item in the account menu, a section of Settings and a link in the About window. All of them go through one piece of code, which does nothing unless the switch `browser.referrals.enabled` is on. That switch is off by default, and Gorilla never turned it on. A test message for developers could also build the address, but never opened it.

**What you see.** The picture shows what happened when we typed about:referrals into the Gorilla build that still had the page: an empty black page. The tab is titled about:referrals and the address bar still holds the typed text. There was no error message and no network request. Here is why. The forwarding code checked the switch before doing anything. The switch was off, so it refused to build the forwarding address at all and answered only "not available". The browser draws an error page for many kinds of failure, but not for this one, so it drew nothing, and the tab stayed on the empty page every tab starts with, about:blank. Gorilla's network locks played no part: the request was never built.

**Does it talk to anyone?** Only with the switch on. Then opening it made a secure (https) request to www.firefox.com carrying your referral code, and the browser noted the click in Glean, Mozilla's data-collection library, which Gorilla never starts. The switch was not locked, so it could be turned on from about:config or by an enterprise policy (rules an organisation sets for the browsers on its computers).

**What we did, and why.** Removed. The browser no longer registers the page, so the address no longer opens anything; the code that built the forwarding address is gone; and the switch is locked off, which keeps every referral menu item hidden.

The referral programme is marketing. Its one technical product is a code that identifies your profile, made to be sent to Mozilla's website. In Gorilla it could not fire unless someone first flipped the switch, but a switch is a latch, not a wall: anything that can change settings can flip it. We would rather not carry a feature whose job is to send an identifier at all. Because the switch was never on, no Gorilla profile ever made a referral code.

**What it costs you.** Nothing. The page invited your friends to Firefox, not to Gorilla. If you want to recommend Gorilla, tell people about it; no code is needed.

**The lesson.** A friendly "share with a friend" button can carry an identifier. The code itself is a string of random characters; what makes it matter is that it never changes and goes to the same company every time. And an empty page is not always a block: sometimes the browser refused before it ever reached the network. Telling the two apart is how you read what a browser really did.

#### For developers

Line numbers are those of the source before the D-157-40 change.

**Registration**

- `browser/components/about/AboutRedirector.cpp:118-121`, listed in `browser/components/about/components.conf:25`. Target https://www.firefox.com/invite/. Flags (upstream): `URI_SAFE_FOR_UNTRUSTED_CONTENT | URI_MUST_LOAD_IN_CHILD | HIDE_FROM_ABOUTABOUT`.
- If `browser.referrals.enabled` is false, the redirector returns `NS_ERROR_NOT_AVAILABLE` before it builds any URL (`AboutRedirector.cpp:210-213`).
- With the pref on, the query is copied onto the target (`AboutRedirector.cpp:244-251`). Because the target is not a chrome page, the redirector tags the channel with its real web address (`AboutRedirector.cpp:263-278`): it becomes an ordinary www.firefox.com page in a content process.

**Who opens it**

- Only `Referrals.openReferralsTab` (`browser/components/referrals/Referrals.sys.mjs:77-88`), which does nothing unless `browser.referrals.enabled` is true.
- Entry points: app menu button (`appmenu-viewcache.inc.xhtml:200-205` to `browser-sets.js:136-137`); Help menu and macOS app menu `menu_referralsPage` (defined at `browser-menubar.inc.xhtml:461-464, 482-484`, handled by `browser-menubar.js:111-114` to `utilityOverlay.js:442-443`, hidden at `utilityOverlay.js:569-570`); account menu "Share Firefox" (`appmenu-viewcache.inc.xhtml:796`; `browser-sync.js:4029-4036, 4106-4109`); Settings section (`preferences/config/account-sync.mjs:822-833, 1138-1147`); About dialog link (`aboutDialog.xhtml:137`; `aboutDialog.js:142-164`).
- A devtools-only test callout (`PanelTestProvider.sys.mjs:36-75`): its button runs `GET_REFERRAL_CODE`, which builds an about:referrals URL but never opens it (`SpecialMessageActions.sys.mjs:1184-1199`).

**Behaviour**

- Generates a 16-character random code, stores it in `browser.referrals.code` and locks that pref (`Referrals.sys.mjs:49-67, 95-104`); the lock is re-applied at every window start (`browser-init.js:688`). `getReferralCode()` returns an empty string while the pref is false.
- Records a Glean event (`Referrals.sys.mjs:81`).
- Opens `about:referrals?ref_key=CODE`.

**Why the probe landed on about:blank with no request**

1. `browser.referrals.enabled` defaults to false (`firefox.js:3835`). Gorilla did not change it and had no diff anywhere in the referrals code.
2. The redirector returned `NS_ERROR_NOT_AVAILABLE` before building any URL (`AboutRedirector.cpp:210-213`).
3. The about: protocol handler passes that error through unchanged; only "factory not registered" becomes "malformed URI" (`nsAboutProtocolHandler.cpp:162-170`).
4. The docshell's error-page filter has no case for `NS_ERROR_NOT_AVAILABLE` and returns OK (`nsDocShell.cpp:6182-6261`). No error page is drawn, so the tab keeps its initial about:blank.

No Gorilla network lock was involved.

**Network**

- Conditional: only with the pref true, an https request to www.firefox.com carrying the code. The pref was not locked, so about:config or an enterprise policy could switch it on.
- Separate and not tied to this page: the attribution "referrals" Glean ping (`AttributionCode.sys.mjs:182-193`).

**Surprising**

- If it is ever enabled, every share sends a persistent per-profile identifier to Mozilla's site.

**What Gorilla changed (D-157-40)**

- The entry is gone from `browser/components/about/AboutRedirector.cpp`, together with its pref gate and query-forwarding code, and from `browser/components/about/components.conf`; the address no longer opens anything.
- `browser/app/profile/firefox.js`: `browser.referrals.enabled` is false and locked. Every entry point stays hidden and `openReferralsTab` stays a no-op, so no Gorilla profile has generated a code.
- Left in place: `browser/components/referrals/` and the entry points, inert behind the locked pref.

<a id="about-blocked"></a>

### `about:blocked`: The red 'dangerous site' warning

![about:blocked](screenshots/hidden-pages/about-blocked.png)

**Removed (D-157-40).** **Talks to:** on click (Google and Mozilla report links carrying the blocked address)

#### In plain words

**What it is.** about:blocked was the full-screen red warning Firefox shows when a site you open is on a list of known dangers: phishing sites (fakes built to steal passwords), sites spreading malicious software, sites pushing unwanted software, or harmful add-ons. The checking service behind it is called Safe Browsing, and it works from block lists that come from outside the browser. Think of the "condemned: do not enter" notice a council inspector nails to a door. The notice is only paper; the inspection decides where it goes. Where the comparison stops: you could tear this notice down yourself, and some of its links would have told the people who keep the lists which address you were visiting.

**When you would meet it.** In Gorilla, never. Malware and phishing checking is locked off, the harmful-add-on list is never downloaded, and no copy of it is built in, so nothing could ever send you to this page. Since decision D-157-40 the page is gone as well: the address no longer opens anything.

**What you see.** The picture (about-blocked.png) was taken on the build before this change (build 28), by typing about:blocked with no blocked site behind it. The whole page is red. In the middle sits a white circle with a red bar across it, a no-entry sign, and below it two buttons: **Go back**, which took you to your home page, and **See details**, which showed the explanation. Because no site was blocked, there is no heading and no text. With a real block a third choice, **Ignore the risk**, let you through for the rest of the session: it reloaded the site past the check and showed a warning bar.

**Does it talk to anyone?** It contacted no one on its own. When clicked, several of its links went out, and some carried the blocked site's address with them:

- a Google page with a diagnosis of the site;
- "report a mistake" links to Mozilla (addresses under phish-error.mozilla.com and malware-error.mozilla.com) or to Google (safebrowsing.google.com);
- information pages at antiphishing.org, Google's unwanted-software policy, Mozilla's support site (support.mozilla.org) and Google's developer site (developers.google.com).

**What we did, and why.** Removed (decision D-157-40). Safe Browsing depends on lists that someone outside your computer compiles and the browser fetches, which makes it a channel controlled by whoever keeps the lists; it was locked off in Gorilla before this change. That left a page that could never appear but was still in the browser: anyone could open it by typing its address, and its links pointed at Google and Mozilla. A door that leads nowhere is still a door, so it is gone. Its own files (the page, its script and its styling) are no longer packaged either. That closes a second way in: in Firefox a page's file can be opened directly by its internal chrome:// address. Only its text file remains, and nothing uses it. From the new build on, typing about:blocked is expected to bring up the network error page's "Hmm. That address doesn't look right." screen, the one for addresses that no page answers to (see about:neterror); this is still to be confirmed on that build. If Safe Browsing ever came back, this page would have to come back with it.

**What it costs you.** Nothing from removing the page: it could not appear. The real cost was paid earlier, when the checking was switched off: Gorilla does not warn you, from these lists, before you open a known phishing or malware site, and does not check add-ons against the harmful-add-on list.

**The lesson.** A warning page is the visible end of a list someone else keeps. Whoever keeps the list decides what you are warned about, and the warning's own links lead back to them. When you switch such a service off, remove what it leaves behind as well: a page that can no longer be triggered is still code that runs when someone types its address.

#### For developers

Line numbers below are those of the source before the D-157-40 change.

- **Registration (until D-157-40).** `browser/components/about/AboutRedirector.cpp` and `browser/components/about/components.conf`, flags `URI_SAFE_FOR_UNTRUSTED_CONTENT | URI_CAN_LOAD_IN_CHILD | ALLOW_SCRIPT | HIDE_FROM_ABOUTABOUT` (as in the unpatched Firefox 157 source).
- **What opened it.** Docshell switches to `blocked` for phishing, malware, unwanted, harmful and harmful-add-on errors (`docshell/base/nsDocShell.cpp:3496-3526`; `modules/libpref/init/all.js:3413`) and adds `&o=1` when overriding is allowed (`nsDocShell.cpp:3848-3851`).
- **Why it could not appear in Gorilla.** Malware and phishing checking is locked off (`browser/app/profile/firefox.js:4092-4093`, gating `netwerk/url-classifier/UrlClassifierFeaturePhishingProtection.cpp:26-30`). The harmful-add-on list (`all.js:3364`) can never be downloaded (`toolkit/components/url-classifier/nsUrlClassifierStreamUpdater.cpp:277-280`), and there is no built-in copy (`services/settings/dumps/main/`).
- **Controls.** Go back loads the home page (`browser/actors/BlockedSiteParent.sys.mjs:152-159`). See details shows the explanation (`browser/base/content/blockedSite.js:77-80`). Ignore the risk grants a session permission, reloads past the check and shows a warning bar (`BlockedSiteParent.sys.mjs:173-297`).
- **Network, on click only; several links carry the blocked URL.** Google diagnostic link (`browser/actors/BlockedSiteChild.sys.mjs:53-61`; `all.js:3458`). Report a mistake via `*.phish-error.mozilla.com` / `*.malware-error.mozilla.com` or safebrowsing.google.com (`BlockedSiteChild.sys.mjs:65-92`; `all.js:3459-3460`). antiphishing.org, Google's unwanted-software policy, SUMO and a developers.google.com advisory (`BlockedSiteChild.sys.mjs:76-144`). The help link opens support.mozilla.org (`:96-102`).
- **Other code.** Only checks the URL prefix (`browser/base/content/browser-safebrowsing.js:14,86`; `browser/actors/ClickHandlerChild.sys.mjs:80`).
- **Gorilla change (D-157-40).** Registration removed from `browser/components/about/AboutRedirector.cpp` and `browser/components/about/components.conf`. The research classed the page removable as configured, and essential again if Safe Browsing returned.
- **Gorilla change (D-157-40, second round).** The page's own files are no longer packaged: `blockedSite.xhtml` and `blockedSite.js` (`browser/base/jar.mn`) and `blockedSite.css` (`browser/themes/shared/jar.inc.mn`). Their chrome:// addresses, a second way into the page from the address bar, therefore open nothing either. `blockedSite.ftl` remains as inert text.
- **After the change.** about:blocked is expected to land on about:neterror with `malformedURI`, like any unregistered about: address; still to be confirmed on the build carrying both rounds.

<a id="about-restricted"></a>

### `about:restricted`: The parental controls 'restricted content' page

![about:restricted](screenshots/hidden-pages/about-restricted.png)

**Removed (D-157-40).** **Talks to:** none

#### In plain words

**What it is.** about:restricted was the "Restricted Content" page of parental controls. Some websites label themselves as adult content with a hidden tag in the page. When parental controls were in force, Firefox stopped such a page and showed this one instead. Think of a cinema usher turning away anyone under age from a film rated for adults only. Where the comparison stops: a film is rated by a board, whereas here each website rates itself, so only the sites that chose to carry the label were ever stopped; a site without the label went straight through.

**When you would meet it.** In Gorilla, never in normal use. It could appear only if parental controls were enforced, which Firefox does in one of two ways: a hidden preference, security.restrict_to_adults.always, switched on by hand in about:config; or the operating system's own parental controls, read through a part of the browser that Gorilla is built without. Since decision D-157-40 nothing enforces parental controls at all, and the page is gone: the address no longer opens anything.

**What you see.** The picture (about-restricted.png) was taken on the build before this change (build 28), by typing about:restricted. A yellow warning triangle sits beside the heading "Error: Restricted Content". Two sentences follow: the page you tried to visit marked itself as adult content and Gorilla Unleashed is set not to show you that content; and the site was blocked because parental controls are on, which you can switch off if you have administrator access. One button: **Go Back**. With a real block, the page also named the site.

**Does it talk to anyone?** It contacts no one. The page could load only the browser's own built-in files, and it had no links.

**What we did, and why.** Removed (decision D-157-40), together with the code that decided whether to enforce parental controls. Gorilla is built without parental controls, so the page served a feature that is not there. Reading the code, the research also found a worse problem upstream: if one hidden preference, security.restrict_to_adults.respect_platform, was switched on in a build without parental controls (such as Gorilla's), the browser asked for the parental-controls part, got nothing back, and used that nothing without checking. That code runs every time the browser creates a new top-level browsing context (the container a tab's page lives in), so the main browser process would crash. This was found by reading the code, not by running it. In Gorilla the check now always answers "do not enforce", so that path is gone. The page's own files (the page, its script, its styling and its draft text) are no longer packaged either, so its internal chrome:// address, a second way in that Firefox allows from the address bar, cannot open it. From the new build on, typing about:restricted is expected to bring up the network error page's "Hmm. That address doesn't look right." screen (see about:neterror); this is still to be confirmed on that build.

**What it costs you.** If you had switched on security.restrict_to_adults.always, it no longer blocks anything. Otherwise, nothing: Gorilla offers no parental controls of its own.

**The lesson.** A label that a website puts on itself is a request, not a guarantee: filtering that relies on sites rating themselves stops only the honest ones. And code for a feature you do not use does not become harmless by sitting idle: here, one setting could have turned idle code into a crash of the whole browser.

#### For developers

Line numbers below are those of the source before the D-157-40 change.

- **Registration (until D-157-40).** `docshell/base/nsAboutRedirector.cpp` and `docshell/build/components.conf`, flags `URI_SAFE_FOR_UNTRUSTED_CONTENT | URI_CAN_LOAD_IN_CHILD | ALLOW_SCRIPT | HIDE_FROM_ABOUTABOUT` (as in the unpatched Firefox 157 source).
- **What opened it.** A `<meta name="rating">` declaring adult content (`dom/base/Document.cpp:12122-12136`) stops the load (`docshell/base/nsDocShell.cpp:4117-4126,3557-3562`), but only when parental controls are enforced. `docshell/base/CanonicalBrowsingContext.cpp:3837-3851` decides: either `security.restrict_to_adults.always` (default false, `modules/libpref/init/StaticPrefList.yaml:19469-19472`) or the operating system's parental-controls service, which is not built into Gorilla (`toolkit/components/build/components.conf:174-182`; `--disable-parental-controls` in the Gorilla repository's `config/mozconfig.win64:152`, confirmed by the build's `config.status:60`).
- **Page.** Shows the host (`toolkit/content/aboutRestricted/aboutRestricted.mjs:16-29`) and a single Go Back button (`:35-37` → `toolkit/actors/AboutRestrictedParent.sys.mjs:14-15`). Chrome resources only (`aboutRestricted.html:7-10`); no links. Network: none.
- **Latent upstream crash.** With `security.restrict_to_adults.respect_platform` set true, the service lookup returns nothing in this configuration and the result is used without a check (`CanonicalBrowsingContext.cpp:3843-3845`); `nsHttpHandler.cpp:552-554` does check. The code runs whenever a top-level browsing context is created (`docshell/base/BrowsingContext.cpp:500-508`), so the parent process would crash. Found by reading the code, not by running it.
- **Gorilla change (D-157-40).** Registration removed from `docshell/base/nsAboutRedirector.cpp` and `docshell/build/components.conf`. `CanonicalBrowsingContext::ShouldEnforceParentalControls()` now returns false unconditionally (marker `GORILLA D-157-40 (2026-10-08): Gorilla is built --disable-parental-controls`), which also removes the null dereference.
- **Gorilla change (D-157-40, second round).** The page's own files are no longer packaged: `aboutRestricted.html`, `aboutRestricted.mjs` and `aboutRestricted.css` (`toolkit/content/jar.mn`) and `locales-preview/aboutRestricted.ftl` (`toolkit/locales/jar.mn`). Their chrome:// addresses therefore open nothing either.
- **After the change.** about:restricted is expected to land on about:neterror with `malformedURI`; still to be confirmed on the build carrying both rounds.
- **Side effect.** `security.restrict_to_adults.always` no longer blocks anything.

<a id="about-crashparent"></a>

### `about:crashparent`: The address that crashed the whole browser

*No picture: No picture exists: opening about:crashparent would have crashed the whole browser that was taking the pictures, so it was never opened.*

**Removed (D-157-40).** **Talks to:** none

#### In plain words

**What it is.** about:crashparent was one of four test addresses that broke part of the browser on purpose: about:crashparent, about:crashcontent, about:crashgpu and about:crashextensions. Mozilla uses them in its automated tests, to check that the browser and its tools cope when something fails. Think of a car maker's crash test: a real car is driven into a wall, on purpose, to prove that the airbags and the safety cage work. Where the comparison stops: a crash test uses a car nobody is riding in, while these addresses wrecked the browser you were using, with your own tabs in it, and anyone at the keyboard could start one by typing an address. Nothing asked "are you sure?".

How the four worked, explained once for all of them:

- **One mechanism.** All four went through one small piece of code in the browser, the crash channel. When one of these addresses was loaded, that code did not fetch a page; it broke the part of the browser the address named.
- **Who could trigger them.** A website could not: the code refused every load that did not come from the browser itself. But an address typed into the address bar counts as coming from the browser, so a person at the keyboard could.
- **What happened afterwards.** Gorilla is built without the crash reporter, the part of Firefox that writes a crash report and offers to send it to Mozilla. So these crashes produced no report, no report window and no upload. One thing we did not check: Windows has its own error reporting, and whether Windows itself records or uploads such a crash is decided by Windows, not by Gorilla.
- **Why they existed.** For Mozilla's automated test suites. Gorilla is built without tests.

**When you would meet it.** Never by accident; only if you typed about:crashparent into the address bar. Since decision D-157-40 the address no longer opens anything.

**What you see.** There is no picture: opening it would have crashed the browser that was taking the pictures. From the code: the main browser process, the one in charge of all the others, stopped at once. Every Gorilla window closed without a question, and on the next start you depended on session restore to get your tabs back.

**Does it talk to anyone?** It contacted no one.

**What we did, and why.** Removed, with the other three and with the crash channel that did the breaking (decision D-157-40). In our threat model every piece of code that can be set off is a door, and it must earn its place or be closed. These four served Mozilla's test machines, not the person at the keyboard, and Gorilla is built without tests; the most this one could do for you was close every window you had open. The four had no files of their own, so nothing else had to go. From the new build on, typing any of the four addresses is expected to bring up the network error page's "Hmm. That address doesn't look right." screen, the one for addresses that no page answers to (see about:neterror); this is still to be confirmed on that build.

**What it costs you.** Nothing you would notice, unless you test browsers: you can no longer crash Gorilla on purpose to check that session restore brings your tabs back.

**The lesson.** Products often ship with their test tools still inside, hidden rather than removed. Hidden is not gone: an address that is listed nowhere still works for anyone who knows it. Looking for what a program hides, and asking whom it serves, is a habit worth keeping.

#### For developers

Line numbers below are those of the source before the D-157-40 change. This entry holds the shared facts for all four crash pages; the other three refer back to it.

- **Registration (until D-157-40).** `docshell/base/nsAboutRedirector.cpp` and `docshell/build/components.conf:14`. about:crashparent carried only `HIDE_FROM_ABOUTABOUT` and cannot load in a child process (`nsAboutRedirector.cpp:226`).
- **Shared mechanism.** All four use `CrashChannel` (`nsAboutRedirector.cpp:30-78`). Loads are refused unless triggered by the system principal and not from outside the browser (`:256-273`), so web pages cannot use them. Address-bar loads carry the system principal (`browser/components/urlbar/UrlbarParentController.sys.mjs:833,861` → `browser/modules/URILoadingHelper.sys.mjs:843-847`), so a user can type them.
- **This page.** `MOZ_CRASH` in the main (parent) process (`nsAboutRedirector.cpp:39-41`): the whole browser dies, and the next start relies on session restore.
- **No crash report is produced.** The crash reporter is not built (the Gorilla repository's `config/mozconfig.win64:150`; the build's `mozinfo.json:13`); on Windows upstream it would be on by default (`toolkit/moz.configure:3459-3478`). A dummy handler is compiled instead (`toolkit/crashreporter/moz.build:31,138-141`), and about:crashes is not registered (`nsAboutRedirector.cpp:114-117`). So there is no minidump, no report dialog and no upload.
- **Windows.** `MOZ_CRASH` on Windows is a `__debugbreak` (`mfbt/Assertions.h:241-245`). Firefox's own Windows Error Reporting module is not registered (`mozglue/misc/RuntimeExceptionModule.cpp:50-55`), so whether Windows itself logs or uploads the crash is operating-system policy, outside this tree. Not verified.
- **Who used them.** webdriver, marionette, puppeteer and mochitests (`testing/web-platform/mozilla/tests/webdriver/harness/detect_crash.py:14-42`), and GeckoView tests. Gorilla builds with `--disable-tests` (`config/mozconfig.win64:148`); the layout debugger that also uses about:crashparent is not built.
- **Network.** None.
- **Gorilla change (D-157-40).** The four entries are removed from `docshell/base/nsAboutRedirector.cpp` and `docshell/build/components.conf`, and the `CrashChannel` class with them (the decision's check requires `class CrashChannel final` to be absent). Android's about:crashcontentjava was removed with them. The crash pages had no files of their own, so nothing needed unpackaging. From the D-157-40 build on, the four addresses are expected to land on about:neterror with `malformedURI`; still to be confirmed on that build.
- **Surprising.** One typed address closed every window without asking.

<a id="about-crashcontent"></a>

### `about:crashcontent`: The address that crashed a tab

![about:crashcontent](screenshots/hidden-pages/about-crashcontent.png)

**Removed (D-157-40).** **Talks to:** none

#### In plain words

**What it is.** about:crashcontent was the second of the four test addresses explained under about:crashparent: the same mechanism, the same absence of crash reports, the same purpose. This one crashed the process behind the tab you typed it in, one of the separate programs that run web pages (see about:tabcrashed). Every tab served by that process crashed with it. The car crash test comparison from about:crashparent applies. Where it stops for this page: only one part of the car was wrecked, and the rest of the browser carried on, so the damage was one tab or a few, not everything.

**When you would meet it.** Only if you typed about:crashcontent. Since decision D-157-40 the address no longer opens anything.

**What you see.** The picture (about-crashcontent.png) was taken on the build before this change (build 28). It shows the result rather than a page of its own: the tab crashed, and about:tabcrashed took its place. The address bar still reads about:crashcontent, the tab's icon carries a small red warning mark, and the page announces that your Gorilla tab has crashed, with the buttons **Close Gorilla Tab** and **Restore This Gorilla Tab**. There is no crash-report form, because Gorilla writes no crash reports.

**Does it talk to anyone?** It contacted no one.

**What we did, and why.** Removed with the other three (see about:crashparent). It was a handy way to test the crashed-tab page by hand, but it served testers, not people browsing, and a typed address that kills part of your browser is a door with no reason to stay open. From the new build on, typing it is expected to bring up the "Hmm. That address doesn't look right." screen (see about:neterror); still to be confirmed on that build.

**What it costs you.** A crashed tab can no longer be provoked by hand for testing. If you never test the crashed-tab page, nothing.

**The lesson.** Testing how a program recovers is good engineering. Leaving the trigger for that test inside the product you ship is a separate decision, and it should be taken on purpose. In Gorilla it was: the trigger is gone, the recovery stays.

#### For developers

Line numbers below are those of the source before the D-157-40 change. The shared mechanism (`CrashChannel`, the system-principal gate, the missing crash reporter, the test users) is under about:crashparent.

- **Registration (until D-157-40).** `docshell/base/nsAboutRedirector.cpp` and `docshell/build/components.conf:14`; it had to load in a content process (`nsAboutRedirector.cpp:227-231`).
- **Mechanism.** DocumentChannel is deliberately bypassed so that the crash happens in that content process (`netwerk/ipc/DocumentChannel.cpp:169-180`); `MOZ_CRASH` at `nsAboutRedirector.cpp:49-51`. Every tab in that process then shows about:tabcrashed without a report form. `browser/modules/URILoadingHelper.sys.mjs:581-584` lets it load in a pinned tab.
- **Network.** None.
- **Gorilla change (D-157-40).** As for about:crashparent.
- **Picture.** about-crashcontent.png is the about:tabcrashed page this address produced on build 28.

<a id="about-crashgpu"></a>

### `about:crashgpu`: The address that crashed the graphics process

*No picture: No picture exists: opening about:crashgpu would have crashed the graphics process of the browser that was taking the pictures, so it was never opened.*

**Removed (D-157-40).** **Talks to:** none

#### In plain words

**What it is.** about:crashgpu was the third of the four test addresses explained under about:crashparent. It told the graphics process to crash. The graphics process is a separate program the browser can use to draw the screen with your computer's graphics chip (the GPU); if the browser was not using one, the address did nothing. The car crash test comparison from about:crashparent applies. Where it stops for this page: the tab you typed it in did not even show a wreck; its own load failed silently, and the damage happened out of sight, in the part that draws.

**When you would meet it.** Only if you typed about:crashgpu. Since decision D-157-40 the address no longer opens anything.

**What you see.** There is no picture: we never opened it, because it would have crashed the graphics process of the browser taking the pictures. What a person sees when the graphics process crashes was not measured. From the code, the tab itself shows no error page.

**Does it talk to anyone?** It contacted no one.

**What we did, and why.** Removed with the other three (see about:crashparent): a test tool for Mozilla's test machines, of no use to a person browsing. From the new build on, typing it is expected to bring up the "Hmm. That address doesn't look right." screen (see about:neterror); still to be confirmed on that build.

**What it costs you.** Nothing you would notice.

**The lesson.** A modern browser is not one program but a small team of programs, each with its own job: one in charge, one drawing, others running pages and add-ons. Each can fail on its own, and each is a separate thing to protect and to audit.

#### For developers

Line numbers below are those of the source before the D-157-40 change. The shared mechanism is under about:crashparent.

- **Registration (until D-157-40).** `docshell/base/nsAboutRedirector.cpp` (`HIDE_FROM_ABOUTABOUT`) and `docshell/build/components.conf:14`.
- **Mechanism.** From the parent process it asks the GPU process to crash (`nsAboutRedirector.cpp:43-47`; `gfx/ipc/GPUProcessManager.cpp:1227-1233`; `gfx/ipc/GPUProcessHost.cpp:343`), which then runs `MOZ_CRASH("Deliberate GPU process crash")` (`gfx/ipc/GPUParent.cpp:730-733`). It does nothing if there is no GPU process. The tab's own load then fails silently (`nsAboutRedirector.cpp:72-73`).
- **Network.** None.
- **Gorilla change (D-157-40).** As for about:crashparent.
- **Picture.** None: never opened during the picture run.

<a id="about-crashextensions"></a>

### `about:crashextensions`: The address that stopped every add-on

![about:crashextensions](screenshots/hidden-pages/about-crashextensions.png)

**Removed (D-157-40).** **Talks to:** none

#### In plain words

**What it is.** about:crashextensions was the fourth of the four test addresses explained under about:crashparent. Despite its name it did not crash anything: it forcibly shut down every process that runs add-ons (the extra programs you add to a browser, such as uBlock Origin, the content blocker built into Gorilla). Gorilla's add-on system treats this as an abnormal shutdown and counts it towards its limit on how often it restarts add-on processes. The car crash test comparison from about:crashparent applies. Where it stops for this page: a crash test leaves a wreck you can see, while this left the screen unchanged, with nothing to tell you that your add-ons had stopped.

**When you would meet it.** Only if you typed about:crashextensions. Since decision D-157-40 the address no longer opens anything.

**What you see.** The picture (about-crashextensions.png) was taken on the build before this change (build 28), right after typing the address. The tab is black and empty, and its title is the address itself. Nothing on the screen says that every add-on process has been stopped; the uBlock Origin button is still in the toolbar.

**Does it talk to anyone?** It contacted no one. In Firefox the forced shutdown can write crash files if a crash reporter exists, and it is counted in Glean, Mozilla's data-collection library. In Gorilla there is no crash reporter, and Glean never starts, so nothing is written or sent.

**What we did, and why.** Removed with the other three (see about:crashparent). Only Mozilla's GeckoView tests used it (GeckoView is Mozilla's browser engine for Android apps). It also stopped uBlock Origin until its process was started again. How uBlock Origin behaves in that gap was not measured. A typed address that can switch off your protection without a word is a door we close. From the new build on, typing it is expected to bring up the "Hmm. That address doesn't look right." screen (see about:neterror); still to be confirmed on that build.

**What it costs you.** Nothing you would notice.

**The lesson.** Names can mislead: "crash" here meant "stop every add-on". Protection that runs as an add-on lives on top of the browser, and the browser underneath can switch it off without telling you. Know which layer your protection lives in.

#### For developers

Line numbers below are those of the source before the D-157-40 change. The shared mechanism is under about:crashparent.

- **Registration (until D-157-40).** `docshell/build/components.conf:14` and `docshell/base/nsAboutRedirector.cpp:240`; implemented at `nsAboutRedirector.cpp:59-70`.
- **Mechanism.** Not a crash: it force-kills every live extension process. The kill would create crash dumps only if a crash reporter existed (`dom/ipc/ContentParent.cpp:4360-4385,4428-4429`); its Glean count (`:4433`) is inert. The add-on framework treats it as an abnormal shutdown and counts it towards its respawn limit (`toolkit/components/extensions/Extension.sys.mjs:809-853`).
- **Who used it.** GeckoView tests only.
- **Network.** None.
- **Not verified.** How the bundled uBlock Origin behaves until the extension process is respawned.
- **Gorilla change (D-157-40).** As for about:crashparent.
