<a id="about-profilemanager"></a>

### `about:profilemanager`: The new profile switcher's main panel

![about:profilemanager](screenshots/hidden-pages/about-profilemanager.png)

**Removed (D-157-40).** **Talks to:** none in Gorilla (blank page)

#### In plain words

**What it is.** A profile is a complete, separate set of what the browser keeps for you: open windows and tabs, bookmarks, history, cookies, saved addresses and cards, and saved passwords. Gorilla, like Firefox, has a plain manager for profiles, about:profiles, and it stays. Firefox is also introducing a newer "profile switcher", made of four hidden pages, and this entry explains what they share:
- **about:profilemanager**, the main panel: it lists your profiles, lets you open one, create one or delete one, and has a "show at startup" tick box that makes it appear every time the browser starts;
- **about:newprofile**, the first page of a newly created profile;
- **about:editprofile**, the same card for the profile you are using;
- **about:deleteprofile**, the delete confirmation.

Each of the other three has its own entry below, which refers back here. Picture the panel of lockers at a swimming pool, each with a name tag and a colour: you pick a locker, rent a new one and decorate its tag, or empty one for good. The analogy stops at the wall. A locker panel is a board on a wall; Firefox's switcher also reached out to Mozilla. Choosing a theme that was not installed downloaded it from addons.mozilla.org, Mozilla's add-on site; in one configuration the list of themes itself was looked up there; and after you finished making a new profile, a guided tour loaded two pictures from Mozilla's servers.

**When you would meet it.** In Gorilla, never by accident. The switcher has been switched off since an earlier decision (D-157-20), and the menu items that lead to it are hidden. Before this change, two paths were left. A profile list (the profiles.ini file) asking for the switcher at start-up could still open the panel when Gorilla started. And a profile list copied over from Firefox that carries the switcher's own identifier (a "store ID") switched the switcher back on by itself, whatever Gorilla's locked setting said, and brought its menu items back. After this change neither happens: the panel does not open at start-up, and with the setting locked off, a profile list from Firefox no longer brings the menu items back.

**What you see.** The pictures of all four pages were taken on the build before this change, by typing each address into a fresh profile. All four look the same: an empty black page, with the address in the tab and in the address bar. That emptiness is the off switch at work. With the switcher off, the browser refused to build the page and showed no error either, so the tab kept the empty page every tab starts as (about:blank). In Firefox, with the switcher on, about:profilemanager shows your profiles with their names, pictures and colours, buttons to open, create and delete them, and the "show at startup" tick box.

**Does it talk to anyone?** In Gorilla, no one: the pages did not open. In Firefox, the four pages load no pictures from the internet themselves, but:
- **when you click:** choosing a theme that is not installed downloads it from addons.mozilla.org; in one configuration the theme picker looks themes up there as well; the "Explore more themes" link opens that site;
- **automatically:** after you press Done on a new profile, a guided tour loads two pictures from firefox-settings-attachments.cdn.mozilla.net, a server Mozilla uses to hand out files.

**What we did, and why.** All four removed (decision D-157-40). Gorilla had already switched the switcher off, because its tour loaded pictures from Mozilla's servers (D-157-20). But switched off is not gone: the pages stayed registered, a start-up path could still open the panel, and the code waited for one setting to change. In the Gorilla threat model, the company that ships the browser, and anyone who can lean on that company, is the adversary to design against, and every channel that can carry code or data is a door. A tour that fetches pictures from the vendor at a moment the vendor chooses is such a door, and so is a theme shop wired into a profile page. We removed the four pages from the browser, together with the code that only they used, and closed the two paths that were left: Gorilla no longer shows the switcher when it starts, whatever the profile list says, and it no longer switches the switcher back on when a profile list from Firefox carries the switcher's identifier, so the locked setting has the last word. about:profiles, the classic profile manager, stays.

**What it costs you.** No profile switcher with names, pictures and colours, and no built-in profile backup (D-157-20): to keep a copy of a profile, copy its folder by hand. A profile list from Firefox that asks for the switcher at start-up now starts straight into the default profile, and the profile menu items stay hidden. The four addresses no longer open anything: Gorilla shows its "Hmm. That address doesn’t look right." page for them, the same page any unknown about: address gets. Profiles are still managed in about:profiles, which can also delete them.

**The lesson.** A feature that is switched off is not gone. Its pages, its start-up path and its links to the vendor stay in the code, waiting for one setting to change, and here Firefox's code would even switch the feature back on by itself when it found a sign that it had been used before; we cut that too. Switching off is a promise. Removing is a fact.

#### For developers

*Line numbers are those of the source before the D-157-40 change; paths are relative to the Firefox 157 source tree. This entry carries the shared material for about:newprofile, about:editprofile and about:deleteprofile.*

- **Registration (before removal):** `browser/components/about/AboutRedirector.cpp:161-183`, inside an `#ifdef` on `MOZ_SELECTABLE_PROFILES`, which is always set (`toolkit/moz.configure:1098-1099`), and `browser/components/about/components.conf:40-46`. Hidden from about:about (register `was: hidden`).
  - newprofile, editprofile and deleteprofile run in the privileged about process through the Profiles actor (`DesktopActorRegistry.sys.mjs:643-654`).
  - profilemanager runs in the parent process with chrome privileges.
- **about:profilemanager** (`profile-selector.mjs`): lists the profiles in the group; launch one, create one (it then opens with about:newprofile, `:142-150`) or delete one (`:151-155`). The "show at startup" checkbox writes ShowSelector to profiles.ini (`:115-122`). Shown at start-up when ShowSelector=1 (`nsAppRunner.cpp:5692-5694`, `3179-3186`) and from the menus (`browser-profiles.js:350-357`; `preferences/main.js:1000-1007`).
- **Why the pictures are blank:** `browser.profiles.enabled` is false and locked (`firefox.js:3725`; D-157-20). `NewChannel` returned `NS_ERROR_NOT_AVAILABLE` for new, edit and delete when the pref is false (`AboutRedirector.cpp:215-219`), and for profilemanager unless the browser was still starting up (`:221-229`). Docshell does not turn that error into an error page (`nsDocShell.cpp:6182-6260` returns NS_OK, and `3695-3697` has no mapping for it), so the tab keeps its initial about:blank. The profile menus are hidden (`browser-profiles.js:82-96`).
- **Network in Firefox (none in Gorilla):** the pages load no remote images (CSP `img-src blob: chrome:` in all four HTML files).
  - On click: a theme that is not installed is downloaded as an XPI from addons.mozilla.org (`SelectableProfileService.sys.mjs:104-280`, `1055-1067`); with Nova (`firefox.js:2237`) the theme picker looks themes up through the addons.mozilla.org API (`ThemesList.sys.mjs:329-345`); the addons.mozilla.org themes link.
  - Automatic: after Done, the `NEW_PROFILE_APP_MENU_TOUR` callout loads two images from firefox-settings-attachments.cdn.mozilla.net (`FeatureCalloutMessages.sys.mjs:978-1042`, images at 1013-1015). These are the "CDN images" behind D-157-20.
- **Gorilla change (D-157-40):** the four registrations are deleted from `browser/components/about/AboutRedirector.cpp` and `browser/components/about/components.conf`, with the `NewChannel` gate that only they used; `nsToolkitProfile::GetShowProfileSelector` returns false (`toolkit/profile/nsToolkitProfileService.cpp`), so ShowSelector=1 no longer opens the selector at start-up. Earlier Gorilla change: the logo in `profile-selector.mjs:177` changed from `.svg` to `.png`.
- **Not changed:** `MOZ_SELECTABLE_PROFILES` stays on at build level, because about 17 modules import `SelectableProfileService`. The references left behind are harmless: `RemotePageAccessManager.sys.mjs:184-210`, `Policies.sys.mjs:471-475`, `DesktopActorRegistry.sys.mjs:525-527`, `652`, `671-672`. The service still initialises on the first window (`BrowserComponents.manifest:168`).
- **Gorilla change, second round (D-157-40, recorded 2026-10-09):** upstream forced `isEnabled` to true when the profile group had a StoreID, whatever the pref said (`SelectableProfileService.sys.mjs:432-447`), so a profiles.ini from upstream Firefox brought the profile menus back. That forcing is removed in `#getEnabledState` ("GORILLA D-157-40 (2026-10-09): no forcing on."). With `browser.profiles.enabled` locked false, the menus stay hidden. Register: "a profiles.ini from upstream Firefox no longer forces it on".

<a id="about-newprofile"></a>

### `about:newprofile`: The first page of a new profile

![about:newprofile](screenshots/hidden-pages/about-newprofile.png)

**Removed (D-157-40).** **Talks to:** none in Gorilla; in Firefox a tour loaded Mozilla CDN images and themes came from addons.mozilla.org

#### In plain words

**What it is.** about:newprofile was the first page a newly created profile opened with, in the profile switcher explained under about:profilemanager above. On it you named the profile; chose a picture (one of the pictures that come with the browser, or an image from your own computer, cropped to fit); chose a theme; chose whether to put a shortcut on the desktop; and then pressed Delete or Done. Picture filling in the name tag when you rent a new locker at the swimming pool. The analogy stops at Done: a name tag calls nobody, but in Firefox pressing Done here was followed by a guided tour that loaded pictures from Mozilla's servers.

**When you would meet it.** In Gorilla, never: it opened only after a profile was created in the switcher, which is off. See about:profilemanager.

**What you see.** The picture, taken on the build before this change, shows an empty black page with about:newprofile in the tab and in the address bar. The reason is the one explained under about:profilemanager: with the switcher off, the browser refused to build the page.

**Does it talk to anyone?** In Gorilla, no one. In Firefox:
- **automatically:** after you pressed Done, a guided tour of the menu loaded two pictures from firefox-settings-attachments.cdn.mozilla.net, a server Mozilla uses to hand out files;
- **when you click:** choosing a theme that was not installed downloaded it from addons.mozilla.org.

Inside the browser, pressing Done also raised a "profile created" signal for Mozilla's in-browser messaging system, the one behind its pop-ups and tours.

**What we did, and why.** Removed, with the other three switcher pages (decision D-157-40); the shared reasons are under about:profilemanager. This page is where the tour began: a message from the vendor, with pictures fetched from the vendor, at the moment you finish setting up. In the Gorilla threat model, where the company that ships the browser, and anyone who can lean on it, is the adversary to design against, that is exactly the kind of door to close.

**What it costs you.** Nothing you would notice in Gorilla: the page could not open before this change either. Now the address no longer opens anything: Gorilla shows its "Hmm. That address doesn’t look right." page instead, the same page any unknown about: address gets.

**The lesson.** First-run moments, such as welcome screens and tours, are where vendors place their messages, because that is when you are paying attention. A tour is a channel: it decides what to show you, and it can fetch what it shows from the vendor at that very moment.

#### For developers

*Line numbers are those of the source before the D-157-40 change; paths are relative to the Firefox 157 source tree. Registration, gating, the blank picture and the Gorilla change are shared: see about:profilemanager.*

- **Openers:** the first page of a newly created profile (`SelectableProfileService.sys.mjs:1853-1865`); profilemanager's create action (`profile-selector.mjs:142-150`).
- **Card:** name; avatar (bundled SVGs, or a local image cropped into a blob, `profile-avatar-selector.mjs:328-329`, `495-510`); theme; desktop shortcut (`ProfilesParent.sys.mjs:154-167`); Delete or Done.
- **Done** fires the ASRouter trigger `selectableProfileCreated` (`ProfilesParent.sys.mjs:263-286`).
- **Network in Firefox (none in Gorilla):**
  - automatic: after Done, the `NEW_PROFILE_APP_MENU_TOUR` callout loads two images from firefox-settings-attachments.cdn.mozilla.net (`FeatureCalloutMessages.sys.mjs:978-1042`, images at 1013-1015);
  - on click: an uninstalled theme is downloaded as an XPI from addons.mozilla.org (`SelectableProfileService.sys.mjs:104-280`, `1055-1067`).
- **Register:** `verdict: remove`, `network: none in Gorilla; in Firefox a tour loaded Mozilla CDN images and themes came from addons.mozilla.org`.

<a id="about-editprofile"></a>

### `about:editprofile`: The page for editing a profile

![about:editprofile](screenshots/hidden-pages/about-editprofile.png)

**Removed (D-157-40).** **Talks to:** none in Gorilla; in Firefox the theme picker used addons.mozilla.org

#### In plain words

**What it is.** about:editprofile was the profile switcher's editing page (the switcher is explained under about:profilemanager above). It showed the same card as the new-profile page, but for the profile you were using: name, picture, theme and desktop shortcut, plus an "Explore more themes" link and a Delete button. Profile backup also led here: after a profile was restored or copied from a backup, the browser opened this page to show it. Picture the counter where you change the name tag and colour of a locker you already rent. The analogy stops at the catalogue: a locker counter sells no wallpaper, but this page's theme picker was wired to Mozilla's add-on site.

**When you would meet it.** In Gorilla, never: the switcher is off and the menu items that led here are hidden. See about:profilemanager.

**What you see.** The picture, taken on the build before this change, shows an empty black page with about:editprofile in the tab and in the address bar, for the reason explained under about:profilemanager.

**Does it talk to anyone?** In Gorilla, no one. In Firefox, only when you click: choosing a theme that was not installed downloaded it from addons.mozilla.org; in one configuration the theme picker looked themes up there as well; and the "Explore more themes" link opened that site.

**What we did, and why.** Removed, with the other three switcher pages (decision D-157-40); the shared reasons are under about:profilemanager. This page had one more reason of its own. Opening it would start the browser's backup service directly, going around the switch that keeps backup off in Gorilla. Backup is off because its default folder is OneDrive, a cloud storage service (decision D-157-20), and a cloud copy of your profile is exactly the kind of channel the Gorilla threat model closes: it puts your data where the vendor of that service, and anyone who can lean on it, can reach it. While the page could not open, this did not matter; with the page gone, it cannot happen from here.

**What it costs you.** Nothing you would notice in Gorilla: the page could not open before this change either. Now the address no longer opens anything: Gorilla shows its "Hmm. That address doesn’t look right." page instead, the same page any unknown about: address gets.

**The lesson.** A page can wake a feature that was switched off. Switches usually guard the front door of a feature; a side entrance, like this page starting the backup service on its own, goes around them. That is why we count pages, not only switches.

#### For developers

*Line numbers are those of the source before the D-157-40 change; paths are relative to the Firefox 157 source tree. Registration, gating, the blank picture and the Gorilla change are shared: see about:profilemanager.*

- **Card:** the same card as about:newprofile for the current profile, plus an "Explore more themes" link (`edit-profile-card.mjs:686-692`) and a Delete button (`ProfilesParent.sys.mjs:125-134`).
- **Profile backup links in here:** a restore or copy opens `#restoredProfile` or `#copiedProfileName` (`BackupService.sys.mjs:3997-4012`; `edit-profile-card.mjs:165-171`). The page waits for `BackupService.init().postRecoveryComplete` (`ProfilesParent.sys.mjs:111`).
- **Network in Firefox (none in Gorilla), on click:** an uninstalled theme is downloaded as an XPI from addons.mozilla.org (`SelectableProfileService.sys.mjs:104-280`, `1055-1067`); with Nova (`firefox.js:2237`) the theme picker looks themes up through the addons.mozilla.org API (`ThemesList.sys.mjs:329-345`); the addons.mozilla.org themes link.
- **Surprising:** `ProfilesParent.sys.mjs:111` calls `BackupService.init()`, which bypasses the `browser.backup.enabled` gate in BrowserGlue (`BrowserGlue.sys.mjs:1320-1325`). `browser.backup.enabled` is false and locked in Gorilla (D-157-20). This did not matter while the edit page was blocked; with the page removed, this path is gone.
- **Register:** `verdict: remove`, `network: none in Gorilla; in Firefox the theme picker used addons.mozilla.org`.

<a id="about-deleteprofile"></a>

### `about:deleteprofile`: The page for deleting a profile

![about:deleteprofile](screenshots/hidden-pages/about-deleteprofile.png)

**Removed (D-157-40).** **Talks to:** none

#### In plain words

**What it is.** about:deleteprofile was the profile switcher's delete confirmation (the switcher is explained under about:profilemanager above). Before deleting, it counted what the profile held: windows and tabs, bookmarks, history and cookies, saved addresses and cards, and saved passwords. Pressing Delete closed the browser and removed the profile's files for good. Picture emptying a locker for the last time, with an attendant first reading out what is inside. The analogy stops at the bin: an emptied locker's contents go home with you, but a deleted profile is destroyed, with no lost-property office.

**When you would meet it.** In Gorilla, never: the switcher is off. See about:profilemanager.

**What you see.** The picture, taken on the build before this change, shows an empty black page with about:deleteprofile in the tab and in the address bar, for the reason explained under about:profilemanager.

**Does it talk to anyone?** It contacts no one, in Gorilla or in Firefox. The counts it showed were read from your own computer.

**What we did, and why.** Removed, with the other three switcher pages (decision D-157-40); the shared reasons are under about:profilemanager. This page carried nothing out by itself. It went because it belonged to a feature Gorilla does not run, and a page kept for a feature that is off is a page nobody checks. In the Gorilla threat model every channel is a door to be checked or closed, and a door nobody checks is the worst kind.

**What it costs you.** Nothing you would notice in Gorilla: the page could not open before this change either. The address no longer opens anything: Gorilla shows its "Hmm. That address doesn’t look right." page instead, the same page any unknown about: address gets. Profiles can still be deleted in about:profiles, the classic profile manager.

**The lesson.** A delete button deserves the same care as a network door, because it is the one action you cannot take back. A good delete page tells you exactly what will be lost before it acts, as this one did. When a feature goes, make sure a safe way to do its job stays; here, that is about:profiles.

#### For developers

*Line numbers are those of the source before the D-157-40 change; paths are relative to the Firefox 157 source tree. Registration, gating, the blank picture and the Gorilla change are shared: see about:profilemanager.*

- **Content:** counts of windows, tabs, bookmarks, history plus cookies, addresses plus cards, and logins (`ProfilesParent.sys.mjs:168-217`).
- **Delete:** quits and permanently removes the profile files (`SelectableProfileService.sys.mjs:1728` onwards, `removeProfileFiles`).
- **Network:** none (CSP `img-src blob: chrome:`). Register: `verdict: remove`, `network: none`; about:profiles still deletes profiles.

<a id="about-settings"></a>

### `about:settings`: A second name for Settings

![about:settings](screenshots/hidden-pages/about-settings.png)

**Removed (D-157-40).** **Talks to:** as about:preferences

#### In plain words

**What it is.** about:settings was a second name for about:preferences, Gorilla's Settings page. Typing either address opened the same page. Picture a shop with two front doors, each with a different name painted above it, both opening into the same room. The analogy stops at safety. In a real building a second door is a second way in; here the room and its locks were the same whichever name you used, so the second name added no risk, and removing it takes none away.

**When you would meet it.** In Gorilla, only if you typed it. When Gorilla opens Settings itself, it opens about:preferences; it only switches to an about:settings tab if one is already open. The only other built-in feature that opened about:settings, IP Protection (a Mozilla feature), is locked off in Gorilla.

**What you see.** The picture, taken on the build before this change, shows the Settings page itself, with about:settings in the address bar and "Gorilla Settings" in the tab. On the left is the list of sections: Account and sync, Home and startup, Search, Privacy and security, Passwords and autofill, Appearance, Gorilla Downloads, Gorilla Tabs and browsing, Accessibility, Languages, Permissions and data, and About Gorilla Unleashed. At the top, a line says the browser is managed by your organisation. Below are a search box, "Find in Gorilla Settings", and the first cards: "Default Gorilla browser", with a cartoon fox and a "Make default" button; "Account", which says its settings are unavailable, with a "Learn more" link; and "Import browser data", with an "Import data" button.

**Does it talk to anyone?** Exactly what Settings itself can contact, and nothing more: both names opened the same page under the same rules. The companion page on the listed pages records that none of the pages about:about lists, Settings (about:preferences) among them, attempted a connection when it was opened. Its "Learn more" links open a web page only when you click them; which address each one opens was not part of this research.

**What we did, and why.** Removed (decision D-157-40). One page, one name. This closes no door, and we say so: the same page stays at about:preferences, so nothing an attacker could use has gone. The gain is in checking. Gorilla is designed against the company that ships the browser, and anyone who can lean on it; every channel is a door that must earn its place or be closed, and a door can only be checked if it can be found. Every name a page answers to is one more thing a reviewer has to find; our register of pages now has one entry per page.

**What it costs you.** If a bookmark or a saved tab points at about:settings, the address no longer opens anything: Gorilla shows its "Hmm. That address doesn’t look right." page instead, the same page any unknown about: address gets. Use about:preferences, or open Settings from the menu.

**The lesson.** Removing something is not always a security gain, and saying so matters. Here the gain is clarity: in a browser where each page has one name, the pages can be counted, and what can be counted can be checked.

#### For developers

*Line numbers are those of the source before the D-157-40 change; paths are relative to the Firefox 157 source tree.*

- **Registration (before removal):** `browser/components/about/AboutRedirector.cpp:136-138` and `browser/components/about/components.conf:30`. Hidden from about:about (register `was: hidden`). An alias that shows the same `preferences.xhtml` as about:preferences (`:100-101`).
- **Openers:** `openPreferences` only switches to an existing about:settings tab; otherwise it opens about:preferences (`utilityOverlay.js:491-511`). The only other built-in opener is IP Protection (`ipprotection-content.mjs:273`, `277`), which is locked off (`firefox.js:3751`). In Gorilla nothing opened it by itself.
- **Network and data:** identical to about:preferences: the same actors (`DesktopActorRegistry.sys.mjs:274`) and the same CSP exceptions (`nsContentSecurityUtils.cpp:1246-1257`). Register: `network: as about:preferences`.
- **Gorilla change (D-157-40):** the two registration lines are deleted from `browser/components/about/AboutRedirector.cpp` and `browser/components/about/components.conf`. This reduces attack surface by nothing, because the same document stays reachable as about:preferences; the reason is one page, one name.
- **Picture:** taken on build 28, before the change.

<a id="about-performance"></a>

### `about:performance`: An old second name for the process manager

![about:performance](screenshots/hidden-pages/about-performance.png)

**Removed (D-157-40).** **Talks to:** none

#### In plain words

**What it is.** about:performance was a leftover second name for about:processes, Gorilla's process manager: the page that shows how much memory and processor time each part of the browser uses. It worked like an old street name still on a signpost after the street was renamed: follow the sign and you arrive in the same street, with the new name on the houses. The picture shows exactly that: the address bar reads about:processes. The analogy stops at usefulness. An old sign helps visitors with old maps; in Gorilla nothing used the old name, no link, button or menu, so the sign led nobody anywhere.

**When you would meet it.** Only if you typed it. Nothing in the browser linked to it.

**What you see.** The picture, taken on the build before this change, shows the process manager under a tab titled "Process Manager", with about:processes in the address bar. A table with the columns Name, Memory and CPU lists the parts of the browser: the main Gorilla Unleashed process; a shared web process holding the open tab; the process for Gorilla's own pages; the Network, Data Decoder, Gorilla Extensions and Utility processes; and spare processes started in advance ("Preallocated"). On the real page you can end a process or close a tab, and double-click a row to switch to its tab. The buttons that used to record a performance profile are gone in Gorilla (an earlier decision, D-157-36).

**Does it talk to anyone?** It contacts no one. It shows tab titles and the websites they come from, including private tabs, labelled as private, and all of that stays on your computer.

**What we did, and why.** Removed (decision D-157-40). The page itself stays, under its one name, about:processes. As with about:settings, removing the second name closes no door, since the same page is still there. Gorilla is designed against the company that ships the browser, and anyone who can lean on it; every channel is a door that must earn its place or be closed, and a door can only be checked if it can be found. A second name is one more place a reviewer has to know about.

**What it costs you.** The address about:performance no longer opens anything: Gorilla shows its "Hmm. That address doesn’t look right." page instead, the same page any unknown about: address gets. Type about:processes instead.

**The lesson.** Software collects leftovers: names outlive the reasons they were made. Each leftover is a place where a reviewer who checked the main name might not think to look. Fewer names, fewer places to miss.

#### For developers

*Line numbers are those of the source before the D-157-40 change; paths are relative to the Firefox 157 source tree.*

- **Registration (before removal):** `docshell/base/nsAboutRedirector.cpp:176-178` and `docshell/build/components.conf:24`. Hidden from about:about (register `was: hidden`). A leftover alias for about:processes; nothing in browser/, toolkit/ or devtools/ links to it.
- **Alias mechanics:** because about: is not a UI resource, the alias sets the result principal to about:processes (`nsAboutRedirector.cpp:280-309`). The picture shows about:processes in the address bar.
- **What the target does (about:processes):**
  - CPU and memory per process, tabs and subframes with titles and origins, and extensions; private tabs are shown, labelled as private (`aboutProcesses.js:559-575`);
  - kill process / close tab (`:1559-1570`);
  - double-click switches to the tab (`:1192-1206`);
  - profiler buttons hidden (`all.js:3751`); the pref is not locked, but the hand-off is refused (`devtools/.../shared/browser.js:96`);
  - Gorilla no longer draws the browser icon (`aboutProcesses.js:609-612`, D-157-35).
- **Network and data:** no network. Tab titles and origins, kept local. Register: `network: none`.
- **Gorilla change (D-157-40):** the two registration lines are deleted from `docshell/base/nsAboutRedirector.cpp` and `docshell/build/components.conf`.
- **Picture:** taken on build 28, before the change.

## Kept

<a id="about-neterror"></a>

### `about:neterror`: The 'problem loading page' screen

![about:neterror](screenshots/hidden-pages/neterror-connection-refused.png)

![about:neterror](screenshots/hidden-pages/neterror-restricted-port.png)

![about:neterror](screenshots/hidden-pages/neterror-unknown-about-address.png)

![about:neterror](screenshots/hidden-pages/about-neterror.png)

**Kept, changed (D-157-40).** **Talks to:** on click (Learn more to Mozilla's support site)

#### In plain words

**What it is.** about:neterror is the screen Gorilla draws when it could not fetch a page you asked for. Think of the slip the post office attaches to a letter it could not deliver: "addressee unknown", "refused", "no such street". The slip tells you that delivery failed and gives the most likely reason, so you can decide whether to correct the address, wait and try again, or give up. Where the comparison stops: the post office slip is written by someone else, far away, after the event; this screen is drawn by Gorilla itself, on your computer, from text it already carries, and nothing is fetched to show it.

**When you would meet it.** Whenever a page fails to load and no more specific error page applies. It is the default for every failed load: the site's name could not be found; the site refused the connection, cut it off or took too long to answer; you are offline; a proxy (a go-between computer that some networks send all traffic through) failed; the site sent you round in a loop of redirections; the site's own security rules forbade showing the page the way it was requested; or the encrypted connection could not be set up. Two kinds of failure have screens of their own instead: a bad certificate (about:certerror) and a failed HTTPS-Only upgrade (about:httpsonlyerror). Both have their own entries.

**What you see.** Four pictures. The first three show the real screen, produced by real failures on this computer; the fourth was taken by typing the address with no failure behind it.

- neterror-connection-refused.png: a program on this same computer refused the connection. On the left is the Gorilla emblem. On the right, the heading "Unable to connect" and a line naming the address that refused. Under a second heading, "What can you do about it?", come three suggestions: the site may be busy or down for a moment, so try again shortly; if no page loads at all, check your computer's network connection; if a firewall or proxy protects your computer or network, make sure Gorilla Unleashed is allowed to reach the web. Below them is one button, **Try Again**: it switches off offline mode if it was on, and loads the page again.
- neterror-restricted-port.png: the address used a port that Gorilla refuses. A port is the door number of a service on a computer: the address finds the building, the port finds the office inside it. Some door numbers belong to services that are not web pages, and Gorilla will not knock on them with a web request. The tab is titled "Blocked Gorilla Page", the heading reads "This address is restricted", and one sentence explains that the address uses a port normally used for things other than web browsing, so the request was cancelled for your protection. There is no button, because trying again would get the same answer.
- neterror-unknown-about-address.png: an about: address that no page answers to (here about:gorilla-no-such-page, made up for the test). Beside the Gorilla emblem, the heading reads "Hmm. That address doesn't look right.", a line says that Gorilla Unleashed can't connect to the server at about:gorilla-no-such-page, and under "What can you do about it?" the advice is to check that you typed the website address correctly. There is no button. This is also what you should see, from the new build on, when you type the address of a page that decision D-157-40 removed, such as about:crashparent; that is still to be confirmed on that build.
- about-neterror.png: the address about:neterror typed into the address bar, with no failure behind it. The tab is titled "Problem loading Gorilla page" and the page is empty and dark: it has no failure to describe.

Depending on the failure, the same screen can carry other controls that these pictures do not show: a **Restore default settings** button that puts the browser's encryption settings back to their defaults, and on some failures a **Learn more** link. The code also holds buttons for encrypted name lookups (DNS over HTTPS) and for the sign-in page of a café or hotel Wi-Fi network, but both of those features are locked off in Gorilla, so those buttons cannot appear. A Search button exists only in Mozilla's nightly development builds, not in Gorilla.

**Does it talk to anyone?**

- **On its own: in Gorilla, no one.** Until decision D-157-40 it did. When a site's name could not be found, the page made up a guess and looked it up without asking you: for a one-word address it tried www.<word>.com, and for other names the same name with www. in front (www.<host>). If the guess existed, the page offered it as a suggestion. The lookup was a DNS query. DNS is the internet's directory enquiries: you give a name, and it gives back the number of the computer that answers to it. Where that comparison stops: the directory you ask is whichever one your computer or network is set to use, and you never see the question being asked. The guess was a question, not a visit, but the directory, and anyone who watches it or can demand its records, learned a name you never typed. Gorilla no longer asks.
- **Only when you click.** **Learn more**, on the failures that show it, opens a page on Mozilla's support site. Its address is built from https://support.mozilla.org/1/firefox/%VERSION%/%OS%/%LOCALE%/, and Gorilla fills in the three blanks before the link opens, so the address itself tells Mozilla your browser's version, your operating system and your language. Nothing is sent unless you click it, and Gorilla has not changed this link. Some failures link instead to Mozilla's developer documentation at developer.mozilla.org, also only when clicked. **Try Again** contacts the site that failed, which is what you asked for in the first place.

**What we did, and why.** Kept, and changed. The Gorilla project designs against the company that ships a browser and against anyone who can lean on that company: every channel that can carry data out is a door that must earn its place or be closed. This page earns its place. Every failed load depends on it: it is the only way you learn why a page failed, the details of the failure can be read only from this page, and the site-information area at the left of the address bar recognises it by its address. Its one automatic door, the guessed lookup, is closed (decision D-157-40): a question you did not ask should not be asked in your name. The Learn more link stays because it opens only when you click it; its address still carries your version, operating system and language.

**What it costs you.** One hint. When a short address fails, the page no longer suggests the www. version (the "did you mean www.<word>.com" hint). You can still type the full address yourself. Nothing else changes.

**The lesson.** An error page is not a passive notice. In a modern browser it is a small program with privileges: it can reset settings, switch modes and, as here, make network requests while you are reading it. Helpfulness is the most common reason a program talks behind your back: the guess was made to save you some typing, and the price was telling a third party a name you never chose to reveal. When you judge a browser, watch what it does when things go wrong, not only when they go right.

#### For developers

Line numbers below are those of the source before the D-157-40 change.

- **Registration.** `docshell/base/nsAboutRedirector.cpp` (listed in `docshell/build/components.conf`), flags `URI_SAFE_FOR_UNTRUSTED_CONTENT | URI_CAN_LOAD_IN_CHILD | ALLOW_SCRIPT | HIDE_FROM_ABOUTABOUT`: hidden from about:about, scripted, may load in a content process.
- **What opens it.** `nsDocShell::DisplayLoadError` (`docshell/base/nsDocShell.cpp:3303`) chooses the error page. neterror is the default (`:3332`) for DNS failure, refused, reset or timed-out connections, offline, proxy errors, redirect loops, CSP/XFO, COOP/COEP and TLS failures (`:3335-3665`). `LoadErrorPage` builds `about:neterror?e=…&u=…&d=…` (`:3841-3876`) and loads it with the system principal (`:3904`).
- **Rendering.** `security.certerrors.felt-privacy-v1` is true (`browser/app/profile/firefox.js:3143`), so the newer error card is drawn (`toolkit/content/net-error-card.mjs:98-132`, `aboutNetError.mjs:1311-1335`); otherwise the older layout (`aboutNetError.mjs:398-631`).
- **Controls.** Try Again leaves offline mode and reloads (`aboutNetErrorHelpers.mjs:74-77`; `toolkit/actors/NetErrorParent.sys.mjs:601-605`). Restore default settings resets TLS prefs (`NetErrorParent.sys.mjs:616-625`). TRR (DNS-over-HTTPS) and captive-portal buttons (`:606-608`, `:659-683`). The page's privileged calls are limited by `toolkit/modules/RemotePageAccessManager.sys.mjs:108-159`.
- **Network, automatic (removed by D-157-40).** On a DNS failure the page called `RPMCheckAlternateHostAvailable` (`toolkit/actors/NetErrorChild.sys.mjs:127-199`; callers `aboutNetError.mjs:357-361` and `net-error-card.mjs:208,333-337`), which used URI fix-up and `checkHost` (`docshell/base/URIFixup.sys.mjs:578-634,1299-1314`) to resolve a guessed name: `www.<word>.com` for a one-word host, or `www.<host>`. A DNS query only, not an HTTP connection, and made with no user action.
- **Network, on click.** Learn more uses `app.support.baseURL` = `https://support.mozilla.org/1/firefox/%VERSION%/%OS%/%LOCALE%/` (`firefox.js:1653`, unchanged in Gorilla), so the URL discloses version, OS and locale to Mozilla. Some errors link to developer.mozilla.org (`toolkit/content/errors/net-errors.mjs:12-17`).
- **Unreachable in Gorilla.** Captive-portal login needs `&captive=true` (`nsDocShell.cpp:3858-3863`), but the captive-portal service is locked off (`firefox.js:4103`). The TRR-only panel and its firefox-source-docs link: TRR mode is locked to 5 (`firefox.js:4158`). The Search button is Nightly-only (`firefox.js:1449-1453`).
- **Why it cannot go.** `getNetErrorInfo` works only on this page (`dom/base/Document.cpp:1682-1690`), and the identity box keys off its URL (`browser/base/content/browser-siteIdentity.js:923`). If an error page's registration is missing, the load fails and no page is shown (`nsDocShell.cpp:3765-3770`).
- **Gorilla change (D-157-40).** `toolkit/actors/NetErrorChild.sys.mjs`: `RPMCheckAlternateHostAvailable` returns at once (marker `GORILLA D-157-40 (2026-10-08): no guessed lookups.`), so `checkHost` is never reached; the comment names both guesses (`www.<word>.com` for a single word, `www.<name>` for a name with one dot). The Glean events the page records are inert: Glean never starts (`toolkit/components/glean/xpcom/FOG.cpp:155-158`) and its upload pref is locked off (`firefox.js:3923`).
- **Unregistered about: addresses.** An about: address that nothing registers lands on this page with error code `malformedURI` (picture: about:gorilla-no-such-page). From the D-157-40 build on, the removed pages are expected to land here too; still to be confirmed on that build.
- **Surprising.** The guessed lookup ran on page load, without the user asking.

<a id="about-certerror"></a>

### `about:certerror`: The 'this site may be an impostor' warning

![about:certerror](screenshots/hidden-pages/certerror-self-signed.png)

![about:certerror](screenshots/hidden-pages/about-certerror.png)

**Kept.** **Talks to:** on click (support links)

#### In plain words

**What it is.** When you open an address that starts with https, the site proves who it is with a certificate: a digital identity card, signed by an organisation that your browser trusts to check identities (a certificate authority). about:certerror is the warning Gorilla shows when that card fails the check. Think of a border officer examining a passport: if it has expired, is made out to a different name, or was issued by no country the officer recognises, the officer stops you and says why. Where the comparison stops: a border officer can phone the issuing country to ask; Gorilla checks only against the list of authorities it carries on your computer, and phones no one. And unlike at a border, you can overrule the officer yourself.

**When you would meet it.** When a site's certificate has expired, was issued for a different name than the one you typed, was signed by no authority Gorilla trusts, or was signed by the site itself (self-signed: an identity card printed at home). It can also appear when something on the path between you and the site presents its own certificate in place of the site's, which is called interception. For sites that have told browsers in advance to accept nothing less than a valid certificate (HSTS), or that fix which certificates they use (pinning), a stricter version appears with no way to continue.

**What you see.** Two pictures.

- certerror-self-signed.png shows the real warning, produced by a test site on this computer whose certificate was signed by itself. The tab is titled "Warning: Security Risk", with a warning triangle, and the address bar shows a crossed-out shield and "Not Secure". Beside the Gorilla emblem, the heading reads "Be careful. Something doesn't look right." The text says that Gorilla Unleashed spotted a potentially serious security issue with the site, and that someone pretending to be the site could try to steal things such as card details, passwords or emails. Two buttons: **Go back (Recommended)**, highlighted, which returns to the previous page or, if there is none, to your home page; and **Advanced**, which opens the details.
- about-certerror.png was taken by typing about:certerror, with no failed site behind it. The address bar shows the crossed-out shield and "Not Secure", the tab reads "Problem loading Gorilla page", and the page is empty and dark.

The warning has more controls than the first view shows. **Accept the Risk and Continue** stays inactive for a short pause after the page appears, so that a page cannot trick you into clicking it by surprise. Once clicked, it adds an exception: Gorilla will accept this certificate for this site from then on, permanently, unless you are in a private window. **View Certificate** opens the certificate in Gorilla's own certificate viewer (about:certificate), on your computer. **Copy** puts the technical details on your clipboard.

**Does it talk to anyone?**

- **On its own: no one.** Firefox can check whether your connection is being intercepted by contacting Mozilla at mitmdetection.services.mozilla.com. In Gorilla that check is blocked twice: the code returns before making it, and the settings that would allow it are locked.
- **Only when you click.** The help links open pages on Mozilla's support site (support.mozilla.org) about insecure connections, security errors and wrong clocks. They are built from the same support address as the network error page's Learn more link, so they too carry your browser's version, operating system and language. When the certificate belongs to a slightly different name, the page can offer a link to that name; clicking it visits that site. **Accept the Risk and Continue** connects to the site you asked for, under the exception.

**What we did, and why.** Kept. This page is the only explanation you get of an untrusted certificate, and the only way to make an exception for one. Without it, a failed check would leave you with no explanation and no way forward. The door that mattered here, the automatic interception check that reported to Mozilla, was closed before this change and stays closed. What remains contacts no one unless you click.

**What it costs you.** Nothing new from this change. Two older effects remain. First, Firefox's special explanation for interception needs the check that contacted Mozilla, so Gorilla cannot show it; which general warning appears in its place was not measured. Second, one of the page's hints about a wrong clock on your computer relies on the time reported by Mozilla's settings server, which Gorilla never contacts; what the page shows in that case was not measured.

**The lesson.** The padlock is not a promise that a site is honest. It means only that the site holds an identity card signed by someone your browser trusts. That makes the list of trusted signers one of the most important things in a browser, and the override button one of the most dangerous: an exception, once made, is remembered. And a warning page that phones home to help you also tells someone where you were when it fired; in Gorilla, this one does not.

#### For developers

Line numbers below are those of the source before the D-157-40 change.

- **Registration.** Browser layer only: `browser/components/about/AboutRedirector.cpp:60-63` (listed in `browser/components/about/components.conf`), flags `URI_SAFE_FOR_UNTRUSTED_CONTENT | URI_CAN_LOAD_IN_CHILD | ALLOW_SCRIPT | HIDE_FROM_ABOUTABOUT`. It serves the same document as about:neterror.
- **What opens it.** `docshell/base/nsDocShell.cpp:3446-3492` chooses certerror for bad-certificate errors; HSTS or pinned sites get the no-override variant (`:3487-3490`).
- **Controls.** Go Back: back in history, or to the home page (`toolkit/actors/NetErrorParent.sys.mjs:98-115,626-628`). Accept the Risk and Continue becomes clickable only after `security.dialog_enable_delay` (`toolkit/content/net-error-card.mjs:1259-1311`) and adds a certificate override, permanent unless the window is private (`:1222-1233`; `browser/app/profile/firefox.js:1658`); only this page may call that API (`dom/base/Document.cpp:1819-1828`). View Certificate opens the local about:certificate (`NetErrorParent.sys.mjs:641-656`). Copy writes to the clipboard.
- **Network, automatic: none.** The upstream MITM-priming check that contacts mitmdetection.services.mozilla.com is blocked twice: an early return (`NetErrorParent.sys.mjs:152-157`) and locked prefs (`firefox.js:1659-1661`).
- **Network, on click.** SUMO pages connection-not-secure, security-error and time-errors (`aboutNetError.mjs:875-941`), built on `app.support.baseURL` (`firefox.js:1653`), so version, OS and locale are in the URL; and the domain-mismatch link to the suggested host (`aboutNetError.mjs:1185-1192`).
- **Gorilla change.** None in D-157-40; the interception check was cut earlier (above).
- **Surprising.** The clock-skew hint relies on Remote Settings server time (`aboutNetErrorHelpers.mjs:251-264`), which is inert because Remote Settings never syncs (`services/settings/Utils.sys.mjs:108-121`). The interception-specific text shows only on interception errors, which Gorilla can no longer detect.

<a id="about-httpsonlyerror"></a>

### `about:httpsonlyerror`: The 'no secure version available' page

![about:httpsonlyerror](screenshots/hidden-pages/httpsonlyerror-plain-http-site.png)

![about:httpsonlyerror](screenshots/hidden-pages/about-httpsonlyerror.png)

**Kept.** **Talks to:** on click (Continue to the plain-HTTP site; support links)

#### In plain words

**What it is.** A website can be reached two ways: https, where what you send and receive is sealed in transit, or plain http, where it travels open, readable and changeable by anyone on the path. Gorilla's HTTPS-Only mode, on from the start, tries the sealed way for every address. about:httpsonlyerror is the page you get when the sealed way fails. Think of telling your post room to accept sealed envelopes only: when a sender only ever sends postcards, the post room does not pass the postcard on; it stops and asks whether you want postcards from this sender. Where the comparison stops: the post room already holds the postcard, whereas Gorilla has fetched nothing over plain http yet, and asks before the open connection is made. And your yes is not for ever: the page says the mode is turned off for that site temporarily.

**When you would meet it.** When Gorilla upgraded an address from http to https and the https attempt failed in a way the upgrade could have caused. Most often the site does not offer https at all. Because HTTPS-Only is on in Gorilla, you meet this page on every site that still offers only plain http.

**What you see.** Two pictures.

- httpsonlyerror-plain-http-site.png shows the real page, produced by a real failure. A made-up test name was pointed at this same computer inside Gorilla's own settings, so no name lookup left the computer, and Gorilla was asked to open it over plain http. HTTPS-Only upgraded the address to https, and the https attempt was refused. (The test could not use an address such as localhost: HTTPS-Only never upgrades an address that points straight back at your own computer.) The tab is titled "Secure Site Not Available". Beside a padlock with a red line through it, a small heading, "HTTPS-Only Mode Alert", sits above the large heading "Secure Site Not Available". A sentence says that you have enabled HTTPS-Only Mode for enhanced security and that an HTTPS version of the test address is not available; in Gorilla you did not have to enable it, because the mode is on from the start. Then come a **Learn More…** link; the question "What could be causing this?" with two answers: most likely the website does not offer HTTPS at all, and it is also possible that an attacker is involved, so if you visit the site you should not enter sensitive information such as passwords, emails or card details; and the sentence "If you continue, HTTPS-Only Mode will be turned off temporarily for this site." Two buttons sit at the bottom: **Continue to HTTP Site** and **Go Back**. **Continue to HTTP Site** stays inactive for a short pause after the page appears, so that a page cannot trick you into clicking it; then it reloads the site over plain http, with an exception for that site. When the page appears inside a frame (a page embedded in another page), both buttons are removed.
- about-httpsonlyerror.png was taken by typing about:httpsonlyerror, with no failed site behind it. It shows the same text, but the space for the site's name is empty and only the **Go Back** button appears.

**Does it talk to anyone?**

- **On its own: no one.** Firefox has an option that, when the upgrade fails, quietly tries the same site with www. in front (https://www.<host>) and suggests it if it answers. That option is off by default, and Gorilla leaves it off.
- **Only when you click.** **Learn More…** opens a page about HTTPS-Only settings on Mozilla's support site (support.mozilla.org); inside frames, a second link goes to a page about mixed content (secure pages that load some of their parts over plain http). Like the other support links, their address carries your browser's version, operating system and language. **Continue to HTTP Site** makes a plain, unsealed http connection to the site: everything on that connection can be read and changed on the way.

**What we did, and why.** Kept. In the Gorilla threat model a plain http connection is an open channel: whoever carries it can read it and change it, and anyone who can lean on them can ask them to. HTTPS-Only closes that channel by default. With the mode on, this page is the only place that tells you why an http site failed, and the only way to make an exception for one site. Without it, those sites would fail with no explanation and no way through, and the temptation would be to switch the protection off altogether.

**What it costs you.** Nothing from the page itself. The mode it serves costs you one extra page and one click on each site that has no secure version.

**The lesson.** A protection is only as good as its escape hatch. A block with no explanation gets switched off by the first person who needs one old site, and from then on it protects no one. A good block says what happened, names the risk, makes you pause before you overrule it, and limits the overrule to one site. And remember that "secure" describes the journey, not the destination: a sealed envelope can still carry a scam.

#### For developers

Line numbers below are those of the source before the D-157-40 change.

- **Registration.** `docshell/base/nsAboutRedirector.cpp` (listed in `docshell/build/components.conf`), flags `URI_SAFE_FOR_UNTRUSTED_CONTENT | URI_CAN_LOAD_IN_CHILD | ALLOW_SCRIPT | HIDE_FROM_ABOUTABOUT`.
- **What opens it.** HTTPS-Only is on in Gorilla (`browser/app/profile/firefox.js:3935-3936`). When an upgraded load fails in a way the upgrade could have caused, this page replaces the normal error page (`docshell/base/nsDocShell.cpp:3667-3672`; `dom/security/nsHTTPSOnlyUtils.cpp:665-689,805-814`).
- **Controls.** Go Back (`toolkit/actors/AboutHttpsOnlyErrorParent.sys.mjs:14-15`). Continue to HTTP Site has a click-jacking delay (`toolkit/components/httpsonlyerror/content/errorpage.js:154-169`) and calls `document.reloadWithHttpsOnlyException()` (`:114-122`), which only this page may call (`dom/base/Document.cpp:1693-1702`). Inside frames the buttons are removed (`errorpage.js:36-43`).
- **Network, automatic: none.** The automatic fetch of `https://www.<host>` (`toolkit/actors/AboutHttpsOnlyErrorChild.sys.mjs:20-50`) needs `dom.security.https_only_mode_error_page_user_suggestions`, which defaults to false and which Gorilla leaves alone (`modules/libpref/init/StaticPrefList.yaml:5085-5088`).
- **Network, on click.** SUMO `https-only-prefs` and `mixed-content`, built on `app.support.baseURL` (`errorpage.js:28-34`), so version, OS and locale are in the URL. Continue makes a plain, unencrypted HTTP request to the site.
- **Why it stays.** With HTTPS-Only on, it is the only explanation of a failed upgrade and the only way to add a per-site exception; also used by `browser/base/content/browser-siteIdentity.js:185,919-921`.
- **Gorilla change.** None in D-157-40.
- **Surprising.** It dispatches neterror's `AboutNetErrorLoad` event (`errorpage.js:174-177`), for the test harnesses. In the direct-open picture the host is empty and Continue to HTTP Site is absent.
- **Pictures.** httpsonlyerror-plain-http-site.png: a made-up host resolved to this computer through `network.dns.localDomains` (no DNS query leaves the machine) and opened over http; the upgraded https load was refused, which produced this page. A loopback address cannot be used for this test: `nsHTTPSOnlyUtils::LoopbackOrLocalException` always exempts loopback addresses and localhost, whatever `dom.security.https_only_mode.upgrade_local` says. about-httpsonlyerror.png is a direct open.

<a id="about-tabcrashed"></a>

### `about:tabcrashed`: The 'your tab crashed' page

![about:tabcrashed](screenshots/hidden-pages/about-tabcrashed.png)

![about:tabcrashed](screenshots/hidden-pages/about-crashcontent.png)

**Kept.** **Talks to:** none

#### In plain words

**What it is.** Gorilla, like Firefox, runs web pages in separate programs called processes, so that one misbehaving page cannot take the whole browser down with it. When the process behind a tab dies, about:tabcrashed takes the tab's place and offers to bring it back. Think of the fuse box in a house: when one circuit trips, only the rooms on that circuit go dark, the rest of the house stays lit, and you can switch the circuit back on. Where the comparison stops: a fuse trips to protect the house from a fault, while a process can die for many reasons, and this page only loads the page again; it does not find or fix the cause.

**When you would meet it.** When the process behind a tab crashes or is killed. One process can serve several tabs, so several tabs can crash together; those in the background show this page when you select them.

**What you see.** Two pictures.

- about-tabcrashed.png was taken by typing about:tabcrashed, with no real crash behind it. The tab is titled "Gorilla Tab crash reporter". A large heading announces that your Gorilla tab has crashed, followed by "We can help!" and a line inviting you to choose Restore This Gorilla Tab to load the page again. Two buttons: **Close Gorilla Tab**, which closes the tab, and **Restore This Gorilla Tab**, which loads it again through session restore (the part of the browser that remembers your open tabs).
- about-crashcontent.png shows the same page after a real crash of a tab's process, provoked with about:crashcontent on the build before decision D-157-40 (build 28). The address bar still shows the address that caused the crash, and the tab's icon carries a small red warning mark. Text and buttons are the same.

The code has a third button, **Restore All**, for bringing back every crashed tab at once; it is not in these pictures. Neither picture has a form for sending a crash report. That form appears only when a crash report file exists, and Gorilla is built without the crash reporter, so no such file is ever written.

**Does it talk to anyone?** It contacts no one. In Firefox this page can send a crash report to Mozilla. In Gorilla three things stop that: the crash reporter is not built, so no report exists; the code that would send a report gives up before sending when there is none; and the setting that allows sending is locked off (in Firefox it is on).

**What we did, and why.** Kept. It is the only page that brings back a crashed tab, and session restore depends on it. Its one door to the outside, the crash report, was closed three times over before this change: no reporter built, no report written, sending locked off.

**What it costs you.** Nothing. The unused report form and its text are still inside the browser, but they are never shown.

**The lesson.** A crash report is a snapshot of a program at the moment it failed, taken while it was busy with your pages. That makes crash reporting, however well meant, one of the richest channels a browser has. Recovery and reporting are separate things: Gorilla keeps the recovery and leaves out the reporting.

#### For developers

Line numbers below are those of the source before the D-157-40 change.

- **Registration.** `browser/components/about/AboutRedirector.cpp` (listed in `browser/components/about/components.conf`), flags `URI_SAFE_FOR_UNTRUSTED_CONTENT | ALLOW_SCRIPT | HIDE_FROM_ABOUTABOUT`; no `URI_CAN_LOAD_IN_CHILD`.
- **What opens it.** The frame loader fires a crash event (`dom/base/nsFrameLoader.cpp:3731-3750`); `browser/components/tabbrowser/Tabbrowser.sys.mjs:9802-9843` passes it to the tab-crash handler; `sendToTabCrashedPage` moves the tab to the parent process and shows the error (`browser/modules/ContentCrashHandlers.sys.mjs:542-556` → `docshell/base/nsDocShell.cpp:3527-3542`). Background tabs show it when selected (`ContentCrashHandlers.sys.mjs:487-519`).
- **Controls.** Close Tab, Restore This Tab and Restore All (`browser/actors/AboutTabCrashedParent.sys.mjs:43-58`, which calls `removeTab` or the session-restore functions).
- **Network: none.** The report form is hidden unless a crash dump exists (`browser/base/content/aboutTabCrashed.css:5-6`). `getDumpID` returns nothing without the crash reporter (`ContentCrashHandlers.sys.mjs:734-737`), and `maybeSendCrashReport` returns before submitting (`:579-582`). `browser.tabs.crashReporting.sendReport` is locked false (`browser/app/profile/firefox.js:2869`; upstream it is true).
- **Why it stays.** It is the only UI that restores crashed tabs, and SessionStore keys off its URL (`browser/components/sessionstore/SessionStore.sys.mjs:3031-3035`).
- **Gorilla change.** None in D-157-40.
- **Surprising.** The dormant report form and its strings still ship (`browser/locales/en-US/browser/aboutTabCrashed.ftl:13,15`). A harmless regular-expression bug at `aboutTabCrashed.js:35`: the replace never matches.
- **Pictures.** about-tabcrashed.png is a direct open; about-crashcontent.png is the page produced by a real content-process crash (about:crashcontent on build 28).

<a id="about-framecrashed"></a>

### `about:framecrashed`: The icon for a crashed frame

![about:framecrashed](screenshots/hidden-pages/about-framecrashed.png)

**Kept.** **Talks to:** none

#### In plain words

**What it is.** Many web pages hold other pages inside a rectangle: a video player, a map, an advert. Each embedded page is called a frame, and Gorilla may run a frame from another site in a process of its own. When that process dies, about:framecrashed fills the frame's rectangle with a small icon, so you can see that this part broke while the rest of the page carries on. Think of a shop window full of screens where one screen fails: the shop puts an "out of order" card on that screen and the rest of the window keeps playing. Where the comparison stops: this card has no words and nothing to press; it is a picture and nothing more.

**When you would meet it.** When the process running a frame from another site crashes or is killed, and the page around it survives.

**What you see.** The picture (about-framecrashed.png) was taken by typing about:framecrashed, so the page fills the whole tab instead of one rectangle inside a page. It is dark and empty apart from a small red icon in the centre: a folder shape with a sad face. There is no text and no button.

**Does it talk to anyone?** It contacts no one. The page runs no script at all. In Firefox a notification bar can appear alongside it, with a Learn more link to Mozilla's support site and a Submit report button; in Gorilla that bar never appears, because it needs the crash reporter, which is not built.

**What we did, and why.** Kept. It is harmless: a picture with no script and no network. Removing it would only leave a blank hole where the frame was, with nothing to tell you that something broke.

**What it costs you.** Nothing.

**The lesson.** Running parts of one page in separate processes keeps a failure in one part from spreading to the rest; this small icon is what that separation looks like when it works. It also shows the test every hidden page in this document goes through: a page with no script, no links and no network has nothing to hide, and earns its place by being useful.

#### For developers

Line numbers below are those of the source before the D-157-40 change.

- **Registration.** `browser/components/about/AboutRedirector.cpp:69-72` (listed in `browser/components/about/components.conf`), flags `URI_SAFE_FOR_UNTRUSTED_CONTENT | URI_CAN_LOAD_IN_CHILD | HIDE_FROM_ABOUTABOUT`. No `ALLOW_SCRIPT`, so no script runs.
- **What opens it.** Abnormal shutdown of an out-of-process iframe's process → `ShowSubframeCrashedUI` (`docshell/base/CanonicalBrowsingContext.cpp:3309-3346`, also `:2392`) → `dom/ipc/BrowserBridgeChild.cpp:202-208` → `dom/base/nsFrameLoaderOwner.cpp:328-354` → `docshell/base/nsDocShell.cpp:3543-3546`.
- **Page.** An empty body showing a centred crash icon (`browser/base/content/aboutFrameCrashed.html:7-31`; `browser/themes/shared/aboutFrameCrashed.css:5-12`).
- **Network: none.** The accompanying notification bar, with a SUMO Learn more (`browser/modules/ContentCrashHandlers.sys.mjs:48-49,411-430`) and Submit report, never appears without the crash reporter (`:319-322`).
- **If removed.** The result of the load is ignored (`nsFrameLoaderOwner.cpp:346-347`), so the frame would presumably stay blank. The research classed the page replaceable (cosmetic).
- **Gorilla change.** None in D-157-40.
- **Surprising.** The tooltip asks the user to "please submit a report" (`browser/locales/en-US/browser/contentCrash.ftl:10`), which Gorilla cannot do.

<a id="about-sessionrestore"></a>

### `about:sessionrestore`: The page that offers your tabs back

![about:sessionrestore](screenshots/hidden-pages/about-sessionrestore.png)

**Kept.** **Talks to:** on click (restored tabs load)

#### In plain words

**What it is.** If Gorilla crashes, it can put your tabs back when it starts again. Usually it does that by itself. In some cases it asks first, and this is the page that asks. Picture dropping your bag on the pavement: a passer-by gathers everything that spilled and holds it out, and you can take it all back, take only some of it, or leave it and start with an empty bag. If one thing in the bag is what made it split, you can leave that one behind. The analogy stops at what you can see. The visible items are your tabs, but the page also holds, out of sight, a full record of your last session: each tab's back-and-forward history, what you had typed into forms, and your session cookies (short-lived cookies a website sets for one visit, which normally vanish when the browser closes).

**When you would meet it.** After a crash, when Gorilla decides not to restore by itself:
- you started Gorilla in Safe Mode;
- the count of recent crashes is above the limit (the limit is 1);
- the crashed session is older than 6 hours.

Then your whole session is replaced by one tab holding this page. If the only thing open when Gorilla crashed was the "welcome back" page (about:welcomeback), that tab is turned into this page too. Otherwise you never see it, unless you type its address.

**What you see.** The picture was taken by typing the address in a fresh profile, so there was no crashed session to show. The tab is titled "Restore Session". The heading reads "Sorry. We’re having trouble getting your Gorilla pages back." Below it, two short paragraphs say that you can try to restore the session again and, if a tab is causing the problem, untick it first. "View Previous Gorilla Tabs" opens a list of your previous windows and tabs, each with a tick box; you can also restore a single tab from it. Two buttons follow: "Restore Session", dimmed in the picture because there was nothing to restore, and "Start New Session", which opens a blank page or your home page instead.

**Does it talk to anyone?** The page itself contacts no one: its own rules forbid it to fetch anything, and the small site icons in the list come from Gorilla's records on your computer, without a connection. Only when you press "Restore Session" do the restored tabs load their websites, as they would have if nothing had crashed.

**What we did, and why.** Kept, unchanged. It is the only way back to a crashed session: without it, the tab after a crash would show an error and the session could not be restored. The "welcome back" page uses the same code. In the Gorilla threat model, the company that ships the browser, and anyone who can lean on it, is the adversary, and every channel is a door; this page opens no channel to anyone, and everything it holds stays on your computer.

**What it costs you.** The safety net is also a record. To offer your tabs back, Gorilla keeps your whole session, including form contents and session cookies, and this page carries all of it. Anyone who can sit at your computer after a crash can see the titles and addresses of everything you had open.

**The lesson.** A browser that can put your tabs back after a crash must have written your session down before it crashed. Crash recovery and privacy pull in opposite directions, and every browser chooses where to stand. It is worth knowing that the record exists, and what is in it.

#### For developers

*Line numbers are those of the source before the D-157-40 change; paths are relative to the Firefox 157 source tree.*

- **Registration:** `browser/components/about/AboutRedirector.cpp:133-135`. Parent process, chrome privileges. Hidden from about:about (register `shown: hidden`).
- **Trigger:** `#needsRestorePage` (`SessionStore.sys.mjs:7249-7294`), when restoring after a crash, returns true in Safe Mode, when recent crashes exceed `browser.sessionstore.max_resumed_crashes` (1, `firefox.js:1588`), or when the session is older than 6 hours. The session is then replaced by a single tab carrying the crashed state (`:729-742`). A crashed lone about:welcomeback tab is converted to this page (`:743-753`). `browser.sessionstore.resume_from_crash` is true (`firefox.js:1535`).
- **Behaviour:**
  - reads the state from the hidden `#sessionData` field (`aboutSessionRestore.js:58-71`; `.xhtml:65`);
  - shows a tree of windows and tabs (`:82-129`);
  - restores all or selected tabs through `SessionStore.setWindowState` (`:138-198`), or a single tab (`:212-237`);
  - "Start New Session" loads about:blank or the home page (`:200-210`).
- **Network:** none from the page (CSP at `.xhtml:14`). Favicons come from the local store with no connection (`:112-116`). Network only on click, when restored tabs load.
- **Data:** all previous tab titles and URLs. The hidden field holds the whole session: back/forward history, form data (`browser.sessionstore.privacy_level` 0, `firefox.js:1579`) and session cookies (`SessionStore.sys.mjs:5525`), stored as an object (`SessionStoreUtils.cpp:345-351`).
- **Gorilla change:** none. Register: `verdict: keep`, `network: on click (restored tabs load)`. about:welcomeback shares the script (`aboutSessionRestore.js:47-53`). Setting `max_resumed_crashes` to -1 turns automatic restore on (`SessionStore.sys.mjs:7279-7282`), but Safe Mode still forces the page (`:7266-7269`).

<a id="about-welcomeback"></a>

### `about:welcomeback`: Your old tabs back after a Refresh

![about:welcomeback](screenshots/hidden-pages/about-welcomeback.png)

**Kept.** **Talks to:** on click (support link; restored tabs load)

#### In plain words

**What it is.** about:welcomeback is the page you see after "Refresh Gorilla", the repair that removes your add-ons and customisations and puts your settings back to their defaults. It offers you your old windows and tabs back. It works like coming home after a deep clean: the cleaners have packed everything that was on your desk into a labelled box, and the first thing they ask is whether to put it all back or only the things you pick. Where the comparison stops: the box holds only the address and title of each old tab, whether it was pinned or hidden, and its tab group; the pages themselves load again from the websites when you restore them, and the small site icons are not kept.

**When you would meet it.** Only after you start a Refresh yourself. You can start one from the Troubleshooting Information page (about:support), or from the notice the browser can show when a profile has gone unused. Both appear only where a Refresh is possible. After the Refresh, the browser turns your old session into a single tab holding this page, with the list of your old windows and tabs tucked inside the page.

**What you see.** The picture shows the page opened by typing its address, so there was nothing to restore. The tab is titled "Success!" and carries an information icon. The page says "Success!" in large type, then that Gorilla Unleashed is ready to go, then that your add-ons and customisations have been removed and your settings restored to their defaults. A link, "learn more about what you can do.", is there for when the Refresh did not fix your problem. Below are two choices: "Restore all Gorilla windows & Gorilla tabs", which is selected, and "Restore only the ones you want". Choosing the second shows a list of your old windows and tabs, each with a tick box. The "Let's go!" button restores what you chose.

**Does it talk to anyone?** Not by itself. Its security rules let it load only the browser's own files and pictures stored inside the page, and it runs in the browser's main process, not in the processes that run websites. Two things reach the network, both only when you click: the "learn more" link opens a help article on support.mozilla.org, and restoring your tabs loads your own websites again, as opening them would.

**What we did, and why.** Kept. It is the only way back to your tabs after a Refresh. Without it, a refreshed profile would open on an "address not understood" error and your old tabs would have to be recovered by hand. It serves you, it contacts no one by itself, and it sits unused until you ask for a Refresh. In principle about:sessionrestore, the page shown after a crash, could do the same job, because it uses the same script and the same hidden list; the gain would be small, so we left it as it is.

**What it costs you.** Nothing.

**The lesson.** Hidden does not mean suspicious. Many hidden pages exist because they make sense at one moment only: after a crash, after a reset, after an error. The useful test for any page is not whether it is listed, but whom it serves and whom it talks to. This one serves you and talks to no one unless you click.

#### For developers

Line numbers are those of the source before the D-157-40 change. D-157-40 did not change this page.

**Registration**

- `browser/components/about/AboutRedirector.cpp:151-153`, listed in `components.conf:34`. The page is `aboutWelcomeBack.xhtml` (`migration/jar.mn:6`).
- Flags (upstream): `ALLOW_SCRIPT | HIDE_FROM_ABOUTABOUT | IS_SECURE_CHROME_UI`. It runs in the parent process.

**What opens it**

- Only a reset started by the user. That sets `MOZ_RESET_PROFILE_SESSION=1` (`nsAppRunner.cpp:5721-5739`).
- The Firefox profile migrator then converts the old session into a one-tab session containing only about:welcomeback, with the old state kept in the page's form data (`SessionMigration.sys.mjs:31-99`; `FirefoxProfileMigrator.sys.mjs:293-331`, which also sets `resume_session_once`).
- The reset itself starts from about:support (`aboutSupport.js:2081-2115`) or from the unused-profile notification (`BrowserGlue.sys.mjs:521-565`). Both require `ResetProfile.resetSupported()` (`ResetProfile.sys.mjs:55-80`).

**Behaviour**

- `aboutWelcomeBack.xhtml` offers "restore all" or "choose", a tab tree (hidden until "choose" is selected) and a restore button.
- It is driven by `aboutSessionRestore.js`, shared with about:sessionrestore. The script reads the hidden `#sessionData` field (lines 21-76) and restores through `SessionStore.setWindowState` (lines 138-180).
- The migrated state keeps only URL, title, pinned and hidden flags and tab groups; favicons are dropped (`SessionMigration.sys.mjs:43-75`).
- Special-cased elsewhere: C++ form handling (`SessionStoreUtils.cpp:349-352`, `SessionStoreFormData.cpp:150`, `SessionStoreHelper.sys.mjs:62-66`); swapped for about:sessionrestore after a crash (`SessionStore.sys.mjs:743-753`); not wrapped again (`SessionStore.sys.mjs:7258-7262`); treated as an initial page (`browser.js:755`).

**Network**

- Automatic: none. CSP allows chrome:, resource: and data: only (`aboutWelcomeBack.xhtml:15-18`).
- On click: the troubleshooting link goes to support.mozilla.org (`app.support.baseURL`, `firefox.js:1653`); restoring reloads the user's own sites.

**Why it stays (register verdict: keep)**

- Essential for Refresh: without it a refreshed profile opens on an "address not understood" error and the old tabs must be recovered by hand.
- Replaceable in principle by pointing `SessionMigration.sys.mjs:90` at about:sessionrestore, which uses the same script and the same `sessionData` field. The registration (`AboutRedirector.cpp:151-153`, `components.conf:34`), `migration/jar.mn:6`, `aboutWelcomeBack.css`, the welcome-back strings and the about:welcomeback literals in the session-store code could then go. The gain is small.

**Surprising**

- Its telemetry counter (`SessionStore.sys.mjs:747`) is dead in Gorilla.
- Gorilla's only change in this flow is the migrator's icon.
