<a id="about-restartrequired"></a>

### `about:restartrequired`: The page that asks for a restart

![about:restartrequired](screenshots/hidden-pages/about-restartrequired.png)

**Kept.** **Talks to:** none

#### In plain words

**What it is.** A browser is not one program but a team of separate programs, called processes, working together: one runs the window, others run the websites. They must all be the same version. If the browser's files on your computer are replaced while it is running, a newly started process comes from the new files and no longer matches the rest. Gorilla then refuses to use it and shows this page. Think of a choir handed new sheet music halfway through a concert: singers who arrive late carry the new edition, the others the old one, and the conductor stops and starts again so that everyone sings from the same page. The analogy stops at carrying on. A choir could struggle through with two editions; the browser will not run mismatched parts at all, so the tab that needed the new part shows this page instead.

**When you would meet it.** When a new Gorilla build is installed while Gorilla is still open, and a tab then needs a new process. The page's words speak of an update that "started in the background". Gorilla never updates itself: updates are pulled and installed when you decide, never pushed. So in Gorilla, the update this page speaks of is always a new build that was installed over the running one.

**What you see.** The tab is titled "Restart Required". The heading reads "Restart to Keep Using Gorilla Unleashed". Below it: "An update to Gorilla Unleashed started in the background. You’ll need to restart to finish the update." and "Your Gorilla windows and Gorilla tabs will be quickly restored, but private ones will not." There is one button, "Restart Gorilla Unleashed". It closes Gorilla and starts it again; after the restart, the tab goes back to the address it was trying to open.

**Does it talk to anyone?** It contacts no one. Its own rules allow it to load only the browser's built-in files.

**What we did, and why.** Kept, unchanged. It is rarely seen, but it is the only explanation the browser gives for this situation: without it, the tab would be left blank and marked as crashed, with no word of why. In the Gorilla threat model, the company that ships the browser, and anyone who can lean on it, is the adversary, and every channel that can carry code or data is a door to be closed unless it earns its place. This page carries nothing in or out, so it is no door at all.

**What it costs you.** Nothing, apart from the restart itself when it appears. Private windows are not restored, as the page says.

**The lesson.** In Gorilla, an update is something you do, not something done to you. This page is the one place where your own installation shows up inside the browser, and the response is a single restart button: no download, no account, no connection.

#### For developers

*Line numbers are those of the source before the D-157-40 change; paths are relative to the Firefox 157 source tree.*

- **Registration:** `browser/components/about/AboutRedirector.cpp:122-123`. Privileged, parent process. Hidden from about:about (register `shown: hidden`).
- **Trigger:** a new content process with a different build ID, because the files on disk changed under the running browser.
  - detection: `nsFrameLoader.cpp:3635-3660`, `3726-3745`;
  - handling: `Tabbrowser.sys.mjs:9821-9843` → `ContentCrashHandlers.sys.mjs:521-532`;
  - the docshell then builds `about:restartrequired?e=…&u=…` (`nsDocShell.cpp:3547-3549`, `3841-3856`).
  - `MOZ_FORCE_BUILDID_MISMATCH=1` forces it (`nsFrameLoader.cpp:3636-3641`).
  - Gorilla has updates disabled, so in Gorilla the trigger is a new build installed over a running one.
- **Behaviour:** one button, `Services.startup.quit(eRestart|eAttemptQuit)` (`aboutRestartRequired.js:21-36`). Session store puts the original URL back from `u=` (`TabState.sys.mjs:253-284`).
- **Network and data:** none (CSP `default-src chrome:`, `.xhtml:9-12`).
- **Gorilla change:** none. Register: `verdict: keep`, `network: none`. Classed ESSENTIAL as a rarely seen safety net: without it the error page fails and the tab is left blank and marked crashed, with no explanation. The only replacement would be changing `ContentCrashHandlers` to use about:tabcrashed.

<a id="about-reader"></a>

### `about:reader`: Reader View, the clean reading page

![about:reader](screenshots/hidden-pages/about-reader.png)

**Kept.** **Talks to:** automatic (the images and media the article names, from any host; a re-fetch of the article with its cookies when it is not cached)

#### In plain words

**What it is.** Reader View takes an article and shows only its text and pictures, in one clean column, without adverts, menus and side panels. It is like a large-print copy of a newspaper article: the same words and photographs, on plain paper, in print you choose. The analogy stops at where the copy comes from. A large-print copy is made once and handed to you. Reader View still loads the article's pictures from wherever the article keeps them, and when it has no copy to hand it goes back to the website and fetches the article again, showing that website your cookies for it, as a normal visit would.

**When you would meet it.** When you ask for it:
- the Reader View button in the address bar, which appears when a page looks like an article;
- the View menu, or Ctrl+Alt+R;
- an add-on that opens it;
- a tab that was in Reader View, brought back by session restore.

**What you see.** The picture was taken by typing the address with no article named, so there is nothing to show: an empty dark grey page under a tab titled about:reader. With an article, the page shows its title and text in one column, with controls to close Reader View, change the text and layout, change the theme and colours, and Read Aloud. Read Aloud uses the speech engine built into Windows, on your own computer.

**Does it talk to anyone?** Yes, but only the article's side of the web:
- **Automatically:** the article's pictures and media load from whatever addresses the article names, which may be other websites than the article's own.
- **Automatically:** when there is no copy of the article to hand (you reload it, you come back to it through history, the tab was restored, or an add-on opened it), Gorilla downloads the article again, with the cookies Gorilla keeps for that website and only those, and follows any redirects.
- **When you leave Reader View:** the original page is loaded again.

It contains no Mozilla addresses. It shows only the current article, in the same sealed-off part of the browser (the "process") as that website. The small site icon comes from Gorilla's own records on your computer.

**What we did, and why.** Kept. Reader View is a feature you choose, and it reaches only addresses the article itself names; it opens no channel to Mozilla. In the Gorilla threat model the adversary is the company that ships the browser, and anyone who can lean on it, and every channel is a door. Reader View's doors lead back to the website you chose to read and the places that website keeps its pictures, not to the browser's maker. We state its two network habits, the pictures and the re-download with cookies, instead of hiding them.

**What it costs you.** In the cases listed above, an extra download of the article with your cookies for that website, so the website sees you load the article again. Leaving Reader View reloads the page. Gorilla is also set to include addresses in Reader View's error messages, which go to the Browser Console, a log on your own computer.

**The lesson.** A feature that looks as if it only rearranges what is already on screen can still go back to the network. Ask of any feature: does it use what I already have, or does it fetch again, and with what about me attached? Reader View sometimes fetches again, with your cookies, from the article's own side of the web.

#### For developers

*Line numbers are those of the source before the D-157-40 change; paths are relative to the Firefox 157 source tree.*

- **Registration:** `browser/components/about/AboutRedirector.cpp:114-117` and `browser/components/about/components.conf:24`. Flags `URI_SAFE_FOR_UNTRUSTED_CONTENT` and `URI_MUST_LOAD_IN_CHILD`, without `MAKE_LINKABLE`, so websites cannot link to it. Hidden from about:about (register `shown: hidden`).
- **Openers:** the Reader View button (`navigator-toolbox.inc.xhtml:374-380`); View menu and Ctrl+Alt+R (`browser-menubar.inc.xhtml:182-183`, `browser-sets.inc.xhtml:250-251`); extensions (`ext-tabs.js:742-744`); session restore (`RestoreTabContentObserver.cpp:87-92`). Path: `AboutReaderParent.toggleReaderMode` (`:211-224`) → the child parses and caches the article (`AboutReaderChild.sys.mjs:39-55`) → the parent navigates to `about:reader?url=…` (`AboutReaderParent.sys.mjs:84-87`, `238-245`; `ReaderMode.sys.mjs:55-66`). The button appears when a page looks readable (`AboutReaderChild.sys.mjs:233-241`; `reader.parse-on-load.enabled`, `all.js:3530`).
- **Behaviour:** accepts only http, https and file URLs (`AboutReader.sys.mjs:86-103`) and falls back to about:blank otherwise (`:101`); shows the cached article or downloads it (`:1249-1290`); offers close, text and layout, theme and colours, and Read Aloud (`:415-416`). Read Aloud uses the local Windows speech engine (`dom/media/webspeech/synth/windows/SapiService.cpp`). The favicon comes from local Places data (`AboutReaderParent.sys.mjs:98-115`).
- **Network, automatic:**
  - CSP `img-src data: *; media-src *` (`aboutReader.html:10-11`): the article's images and media load from any host.
  - With no cached article (reload, restore, history, extension), an XHR fetches the page again **with cookies** (`mozAnon:false`, first-party isolated) and follows redirects (`ReaderMode.sys.mjs:224-245`; `AboutReader.sys.mjs:1266-1275`).
  - Leaving Reader View reloads the original page (`ReaderMode.sys.mjs:73-118`).
- **Scope:** no Mozilla URLs. It shows the current article only, in that site's process (`ProcessIsolation.cpp:192`, `436-460`). `reader.errors.includeURLs=true` (`firefox.js:2908`) writes URLs to the Browser Console.
- **Gorilla change:** none. Register: `verdict: keep`, `network: automatic (the images and media the article names, from any host; a re-fetch of the article with its cookies when it is not cached)`. Removal would take the whole feature: delete `AboutRedirector.cpp:114-117` and `components.conf:24`, set `reader.parse-on-load.enabled=false`, remove the AboutReader actor (`DesktopActorRegistry.sys.mjs:181-197`) and the menu entry and key (`browser-sets.inc.xhtml:48`, `250-251`). Print's "Simplify page" calls `ReaderMode.parseDocument` directly (`PrintingChild.sys.mjs:81-116`) and would keep working.
- **Surprising:** the cookie-bearing re-download described above.

<a id="about-opentabs"></a>

### `about:opentabs`: Split View's 'choose a tab' pane

![about:opentabs](screenshots/hidden-pages/about-opentabs.png)

**Kept.** **Talks to:** none

#### In plain words

**What it is.** Split View shows two tabs side by side in one window. When you start a split, the second half needs a tab, and about:opentabs is the pane that lets you choose it. It works like laying papers side by side on a desk: one is in front of you, and you point at the pile to choose the one that goes next to it. The analogy stops at the pile. On a desk you can pick any paper in the room; this pane lists only the tabs of the current window that are not pinned and not already in a split.

**When you would meet it.** When you start a Split View: with the Add Split View command or its keyboard shortcut, or from the menu that opens when you right-click a tab.

**What you see.** Opened by typing its address, outside a split, it does not show its list: it sends you to the new tab page. That is what the picture shows: Gorilla's new tab page, with the Gorilla logo in the centre, a "Search the web" box below it, a line at the top about placing bookmarks on the bookmarks toolbar, and a tab titled "New Gorilla Tab". Inside a split, the pane lists the tabs you can choose, with a search box; clicking one puts it into the other half.

**Does it talk to anyone?** It contacts no one. Its rules allow pictures only from inside the browser, and the small site icons come from Gorilla's local cache without a connection. The tab titles and addresses it lists never leave your computer.

**What we did, and why.** Kept. Split View is switched on in Gorilla, and this pane is part of it. It could be replaced by sending its three openers to the new tab page and removing the checks for its address in several places, but nothing would be gained: it opens no channel to Mozilla or anyone else. In the Gorilla threat model, the company that ships the browser, and anyone who can lean on it, is the adversary, and a door is any channel that can carry code or data out; this pane has none. It does run with the browser's full privileges, because it reaches into the window to move tabs, and that is exactly why it matters that it touches nothing outside your computer.

**What it costs you.** Nothing.

**The lesson.** Some of what looks like the browser's own controls is built from web pages. Those pages run with full power over the browser, so the safe ones are those that touch nothing outside your computer. When you check a browser, the hidden pages that form part of its controls deserve as much attention as the ones that show websites.

#### For developers

*Line numbers are those of the source before the D-157-40 change; paths are relative to the Firefox 157 source tree.*

- **Registration:** `browser/components/about/AboutRedirector.cpp:95-97`. Parent process with the system principal; it reaches into the chrome window (`opentabs-splitview.mjs:36-44`). Hidden from about:about (register `shown: hidden`).
- **Openers:**
  - the Add Split View command and its shortcut (`browser-commands.js:85-101`; `browser-sets.inc.xhtml:375`);
  - the tab context menu (`tab-context-menu.js:1388-1392`);
  - the message action `OPEN_TAB_IN_SPLITVIEW` (`SpecialMessageActions.sys.mjs:902-906`).
- **Behaviour:** lists the window's unpinned, unsplit tabs, with a local search (`opentabs-splitview.mjs:117-141`); clicking a tab puts it into the split (`:106-115`); outside a split it redirects to about:newtab (`:153-166`), which is what the picture shows.
- **Network and data:** none. CSP `img-src data: chrome:` (`opentabs.html:9-12`); favicons come from the local cache without a connection (`PlacesUIUtils.sys.mjs:1737-1745`). Personal data: tab titles and URLs, local.
- **Gorilla change:** the branding favicon `<link>` was removed from `opentabs.html` (D-157-35). Split View is enabled (`browser.tabs.splitView.enabled`, `firefox.js:2884`). Register: `verdict: keep`, `network: none`.
- **Classed REPLACEABLE, kept:** to remove it, point the three callers at about:newtab and drop the URL checks in `Tabbrowser.sys.mjs:4474`, `10671`; `tabsplitview.mjs:364`, `399-401`; `split-view-footer.js:168`; `tab-context-menu.js:825`; `browser.js:751`.
- **Surprising:** the message action force-enables `browser.tabs.splitView.enabled` (`SpecialMessageActions.sys.mjs:903`).

<a id="about-devtools-toolbox"></a>

### `about:devtools-toolbox`: The frame that holds the developer tools

![about:devtools-toolbox](screenshots/hidden-pages/about-devtools-toolbox.png)

**Kept.** **Talks to:** when used (the inspected site and its source maps)

#### In plain words

**What it is.** about:devtools-toolbox is the page inside which the browser's developer tools run: the Inspector (the building blocks of a web page), the Console (messages and errors from the page's scripts), the Debugger (the page's code, step by step), the Network panel (every request the page makes) and the rest. You open them with the F12 key. It works like the workbench in a workshop that all the tools are mounted on: you never think about the bench, you use the tools, but take the bench away and no tool has anywhere to sit. Where the comparison stops: a bench is passive, while this page runs with the browser's own highest privileges, in its main process, and can read whatever the page you are inspecting exposes.

**When you would meet it.** Every time you open the developer tools, though you never see its address: each toolbox is loaded at it. It shows up as an address in a tab when you press "Inspect" on about:debugging, the page for debugging tabs, add-ons and background workers.

**What you see.** Typed by hand, as in the picture, it is an empty dark page with a small window-shaped icon on the tab. It was not told which tab or add-on to inspect, so it had nothing to show. Opened with F12, the same page fills with the toolbox.

**Does it talk to anyone?** The research found no automatic traffic to Mozilla. When you use the tools, they fetch what the page you are inspecting needs from that page's own site: its files and, where the site provides them, its "source maps" (files that turn a site's compressed code back into readable code). In the toolbox's menu, the Documentation and Community links open Mozilla's web pages when you click them.

Gorilla had already closed three doors around it: a performance recording can only be handed to a viewer running on your own computer (localhost); the Browser Toolbox, which points these tools at the browser itself, is locked off; and the server that lets another computer debug this browser is locked off. DevTools also has no Performance panel in Gorilla.

**What we did, and why.** Kept. Without this page there are no developer tools: removing it removes F12 entirely. The developer tools serve the person at the keyboard. They are how anyone, not only Mozilla, can see what a web page really does: which addresses it calls, which scripts it runs, what it stores. A browser that asks you to check its claims has to keep the instrument you check them with. It contacts no one on its own, and the doors around it that reached further are shut.

**What it costs you.** Not measured. The tools take space in the browser's files, and memory while they are open; we have not measured how much. If you never press F12, they stay closed. If you want no developer tools at all, an enterprise policy called DisableDeveloperTools blocks this page.

**The lesson.** A privileged page is not bad in itself; what matters is whom it works for. This page has more access than almost any other, and it points that access at the websites you choose to inspect, when you ask. Compare about:asrouter, also a console: that one pointed messages at you. The same kind of tool can face either way.

#### For developers

Line numbers are those of the source before the D-157-40 change. D-157-40 did not change this page.

**Registration**

- Not in the C++ redirector tables: a JS about-module component registered in `devtools/startup/components.conf:7-27`, only when `MOZ_DEVTOOLS == 'all'`, which browser builds turn on (`browser/moz.configure:17`).
- `AboutDevToolsToolboxRegistration.sys.mjs:12-31` maps it to chrome://devtools/content/framework/toolbox.xhtml with full chrome (system) privileges in the parent process. Flags: `ALLOW_SCRIPT | ENABLE_INDEXED_DB | HIDE_FROM_ABOUTABOUT`.

**What opens it**

- Every time DevTools opens: every in-window toolbox frame is pointed at it (`toolbox-host-manager.js:135-138`; `toolbox.js:453`; frames created at `toolbox-hosts.js:769-790`).
- about:debugging's "Inspect" opens it as a tab with `?type=…&id=…` (`debug-targets.js:109-111`).
- It reads whatever the debugged target exposes.

**Special-cased elsewhere**

- `ContextMenuChild.sys.mjs:846-857`; `QuickActionsLoaderDefault.sys.mjs:160-179`; `devtools-browser.js` (lines 180, 253 and 451-487); the data: and blob: image allow-list at `nsContentSecurityUtils.cpp:1345`.

**Network**

- Automatic: the research found no automatic traffic to Mozilla.
- On use: the inspected site's resources and source maps (`devtools.source-map.client-service.enabled`, `firefox.js:3467`).
- On click: the Documentation and Community links (`MeatballMenu.js:41-46`).

**Gorilla's existing changes around it**

- Performance profiles may only go to a viewer on localhost (`devtools/client/performance-new/shared/browser.js`); DevTools has no Performance panel.
- The Browser Toolbox (`devtools.chrome.enabled`) and the remote debugging server (`devtools.debugger.remote-enabled`) are locked off (`firefox.js:4116-4117`).

**Why it stays (register verdict: keep)**

- Essential while DevTools ships: removing the registration breaks F12 entirely.
- The only clean ways to drop it are to build without DevTools, or to use the `DisableDeveloperTools` policy, which already blocks this page (`Policies.sys.mjs:1160-1170`).

<a id="about-cache-entry"></a>

### `about:cache-entry`: The detail view of one cached item

![about:cache-entry](screenshots/hidden-pages/about-cache-entry.png)

**Kept.** **Talks to:** on click (the cached address)

#### In plain words

**What it is.** When Gorilla downloads a page, a picture or a script, it keeps a copy, so that it need not download the same thing again. That store of copies is the cache. about:cache, a listed page kept for people who look after networks, shows the cache's index; about:cache-entry is what opens when you click one entry in that index. Picture an office that photocopies every letter it receives and files the copies, so that nobody has to ask the sender again. about:cache is the filing index. about:cache-entry is one copy pulled out and laid on the desk: first the envelope details, then the whole letter. The analogy stops at what gets copied. An office photocopy shows the letter; the browser's copy also keeps the notes that travelled with it, including cookie values a website set, and this page prints them as plain text.

**When you would meet it.** Only if you open about:cache and click an entry. Gorilla never opens it by itself, and websites cannot link to it.

**What you see.** The picture was taken by typing the address with no entry named, so the page is empty: a black page, with about:cache-entry in the tab and in the address bar. Opened from about:cache, it shows:
- the entry's address (its "key"), as a link;
- how many times it was fetched, its dates, when it expires, its size, and whether it came over a secure connection;
- every piece of information stored with it (the "metadata"), including the headers: the short notes a website sends before the content itself, such as cookies it wants your browser to keep;
- the whole stored content, written out as raw numbers (a "hex dump": the bytes exactly as the computer keeps them).

There are no buttons. The only thing to click is the address.

**Does it talk to anyone?** It fetches nothing by itself: its own rules allow it to load only the browser's built-in files. If you click the address at the top, Gorilla opens that address, an ordinary visit to that website that you chose. Looking at an entry does not even change its fetch count, so it leaves no mark in the cache.

**What we did, and why.** Kept. Without it, every entry link on about:cache would fail, and about:cache is the page network administrators use to see what a browser has stored. It opens no channel to Mozilla or to anyone else, so in the Gorilla threat model, where the company that ships the browser and anyone who can lean on it are the adversary, it is not a door. We are plain about what it shows: cached addresses, the headers of requests and responses, and the stored content itself. Set-Cookie values from cached responses (the cookie values websites sent to your browser) can appear in plain text, because one of the stored copies of the headers keeps them. It can also be pointed at the private-browsing cache, which is kept in memory. All of this stays on your computer: the page shows what the cache already holds and collects nothing new.

**What it costs you.** No network and no speed. The cost is on your own computer: anyone who can sit at your Gorilla can open about:cache and read, entry by entry, which addresses you loaded, what the websites sent back, and cookie values from cached responses. Removing this page would not remove that data; the cache itself holds it.

**The lesson.** Your browsing leaves copies on your own computer, in more detail than most people expect. Privacy is not only about what leaves the machine; it is also about what stays on it, and who else can sit down at it. A browser that hides its diagnostic pages does not hold less data; it only shows you less of it.

#### For developers

*Line numbers are those of the source before the D-157-40 change; paths are relative to the Firefox 157 source tree.*

- **Registration:** `netwerk/build/components.conf:285-291`, main process only (line 290). Hidden from about:about (register `shown: hidden`). Its flags lack `MAKE_LINKABLE` (`nsAboutCacheEntry.cpp:108-111`), so web pages cannot link to it.
- **Opener:** only the entry links on about:cache (`nsAboutCache.cpp:368-395`). The browser never opens it by itself.
- **Behaviour:**
  - parses `?storage=&context=&eid=&uri=` (`nsAboutCacheEntry.cpp:201-262`);
  - opens the entry with `OPEN_READONLY|OPEN_SECRETLY`, so fetch counts are not updated (`:193-195`);
  - prints the key as a link, fetch count, dates, expiry, size and whether it is secure (`:315-430`);
  - prints every metadata element (`:437-438`, `482-514`);
  - prints a hex dump of the whole cached body (`:445-468`, `29-79`).
  - No actions apart from the key link.
- **Network:** nothing automatic; the page's CSP is `default-src chrome:` (`:150-151`). Clicking the key link opens the cached URL (`:342-350`).
- **Data:** cached URLs, request and response headers, response bodies. The `context` parameter can name the private-browsing memory cache (`nsAboutCache.cpp:210-232`, `nsAboutCacheEntry.cpp:254`). The values of request headers named in `Vary` are stored, with cookies hashed (`nsHttpChannel.cpp:6435`).
- **Surprising:** `response-head` is flattened with Set-Cookie removed (`nsHttpHeaderArray.cpp:414-425`), but `original-response-headers` is written without that removal (`nsHttpHeaderArray.cpp:454-476`, written at `nsHttpChannel.cpp:6478-6479`). The page prints both, so Set-Cookie values from cached responses can appear in plain text.
- **Gorilla change:** none. The research classes it REMOVABLE (delete `components.conf:285-291`, optionally `netwerk/protocol/about/moz.build:19`, ideally together with about:cache at `components.conf:278-284`). The register keeps it (`verdict: keep`, `network: on click (the cached address)`) as the detail view behind about:cache, which stays for network administrators.

<a id="about-blank"></a>

### `about:blank`: The empty page every tab starts as

![about:blank](screenshots/hidden-pages/about-blank.png)

**Kept.** **Talks to:** none

#### In plain words

**What it is.** about:blank is a page with nothing in it. It works like the blank top sheet of a new notepad: before anyone writes a word, the sheet is already there. Every new tab, every new window and every empty frame inside a website starts as one of these sheets, and the real page is written over it. The analogy stops at ownership. A notepad belongs to whoever bought it; an about:blank page takes on the identity of whatever created it. If a website opens an empty window, that window counts as the website's own page, with the website's permissions and limits. It is not a page of Gorilla's.

**When you would meet it.** Mostly without noticing:
- for a moment, as the first page of every new tab and window, before the page you asked for arrives;
- as your start page, if Gorilla is set to start with a blank page;
- after a crash, when you press "Start New Session" on the restore page (about:sessionrestore);
- when Reader View is given an address it does not accept (it accepts only http, https and file addresses);
- when a website opens a new window with nothing in it, or puts an empty frame in its page.

**What you see.** Nothing, on purpose. The picture shows a black page under a tab titled "New Gorilla Tab". There is no heading, no text and no button. The address bar is empty, as it is for a new tab.

**Does it talk to anyone?** It contacts no one. The page has no content, so there is nothing in it that could fetch anything.

**What we did, and why.** Kept, unchanged. The HTML standard, the rulebook every browser follows, defines about:blank, and Gorilla's own code relies on it in many places: the rules that decide a tab's first page, the browser's list of "nothing loaded yet" pages, and the check that asks "is this page empty?". Gorilla is designed against the company that ships the browser, and anyone who can lean on that company; every channel that can carry code or data out is a door that must earn its place or be closed. about:blank is not a door. It carries nothing in or out. Removing it would break the browser and most websites, and close nothing.

**What it costs you.** Nothing.

**The lesson.** In a browser, even an empty page has an owner. Browser security follows who created a page, not what is written on it. That is why a blank window opened by a website is the website's window, with the website's limits. When you wonder whether something on your screen is "the browser" or "the site", ask who opened it.

#### For developers

*Line numbers are those of the source before the D-157-40 change; paths are relative to the Firefox 157 source tree.*

- **Registration:** `netwerk/build/components.conf:272-277`. Flags (`netwerk/protocol/about/nsAboutBlank.cpp:34-39`): `URI_SAFE_FOR_UNTRUSTED_CONTENT`, `URI_CAN_LOAD_IN_CHILD`, `MAKE_LINKABLE`, `HIDE_FROM_ABOUTABOUT`.
- **Channel:** `nsAboutBlank::NewChannel` returns an empty `text/html` stream (`nsAboutBlank.cpp:14-31`). The about: handler wraps it as a nested `moz-safe-about:` URI so that security checks treat it as safe (`nsAboutProtocolHandler.cpp:91-109`).
- **Openers:**
  - first document of new tabs and windows (`BrowserContentHandler.sys.mjs:385`);
  - start page when `browser.startup.page` is 0 (`BrowserContentHandler.sys.mjs:743-771`);
  - "Start New Session" on about:sessionrestore (`aboutSessionRestore.js:201-206`);
  - Reader View's fallback for a URL it refuses (`AboutReader.sys.mjs:101`);
  - web content, through `window.open()` and `<iframe>` without `src`.
- **Dependants:** `NS_IsAboutBlank` (`netwerk/base/nsNetUtil.cpp:2810`); the docshell initial-document logic (`nsDocShell.cpp:1122-1133`, `2501`); the browser's list of initial pages (`browser.js:747`).
- **Network and data:** none.
- **Gorilla change:** none. Register: `verdict: keep`, `network: none`. Classed ESSENTIAL: the HTML standard defines it.
- **Surprising:** the document takes the origin of whoever creates it (`dom/base/nsNodeInfoManager.cpp:341`, `caps/ContentPrincipal.cpp:134`). What it shows belongs to that page, not to the browser.

<a id="about-srcdoc"></a>

### `about:srcdoc`: The label for frames without an address

![about:srcdoc](screenshots/hidden-pages/about-srcdoc.png)

**Kept.** **Talks to:** none

#### In plain words

**What it is.** A website can place a smaller page inside its own page, in a box called a frame (an "iframe"). Usually the frame shows a page fetched from an address. A website can also write the frame's content straight into its own page, so there is nothing to fetch. That kind of frame has no address of its own, so the browser gives it the label about:srcdoc. Think of an envelope marked "By hand" where the postal address would go: it tells the sorting office that the letter travels with its sender and is not to be posted anywhere. Try to post something to "By hand" and the post office cannot deliver it; type about:srcdoc and the browser cannot open it either. The analogy stops at the courier. Nobody carries anything: the page already holds the text, and the browser builds the frame from it on the spot. The label exists only so that the browser's security checks let the frame through.

**When you would meet it.** Never on screen, unless you type its address. It works behind the scenes on websites that use frames written this way.

**What you see.** Typing the address gets an error page, because the browser refuses to open it, on purpose. The picture shows Gorilla's error page: the Gorilla logo on the left; the heading "Hmm. That address doesn’t look right."; the line "Gorilla Unleashed can’t connect to the server at about:srcdoc"; and, under "What can you do about it?", the advice to check that the address was typed correctly. The tab is titled "Problem loading Gorilla page". There are no buttons.

**Does it talk to anyone?** It contacts no one. The content of such a frame comes from the website that wrote it and loads under that website's own rules, like the rest of that website.

**What we did, and why.** Kept, unchanged. Web standards require it, and the browser's security checks look it up. Without the label, the browser would treat every frame of this kind as dangerous to load, and websites could no longer show them; a large number of websites would break. In the Gorilla threat model, the company that ships the browser, and anyone who can lean on it, is the adversary, and every channel is a door. about:srcdoc is no door: it never loads, it carries nothing, and it opens no channel to anyone.

**What it costs you.** Nothing.

**The lesson.** The web's security is built on addresses: a browser decides what a page may do by asking where it came from. Content with no address still needs a name to be checked against, so the browser keeps a name that can never be visited. This is a page registered so that it can never be loaded, and it is still essential.

#### For developers

*Line numbers are those of the source before the D-157-40 change; paths are relative to the Firefox 157 source tree.*

- **Registration:** `docshell/base/nsAboutRedirector.cpp:200-206` and `docshell/build/components.conf:28`. Hidden from about:about (register `shown: hidden`). The comment at `nsAboutRedirector.cpp:200-201` says it is registered so that it can never be loaded.
- **What uses it:** the URI given to an `<iframe>` with a `srcdoc` attribute (`dom/base/nsFrameLoader.cpp:496-499`). The docshell builds the document from the attribute text in an input-stream channel (`nsDocShell.cpp:9194-9201`); view-source handles it the same way (`nsViewSourceChannel.cpp:119-125`).
- **Never resolved:** `nsAboutProtocolHandler::NewChannel` always returns `NS_ERROR_MALFORMED_URI` for it (`nsAboutProtocolHandler.cpp:125-133`), hence the malformed-address error page in the picture. The entry exists only to supply flags.
- **Why it stays:** without the module the flags fall back to `URI_DANGEROUS_TO_LOAD` (`nsAboutProtocolHandler.cpp:44-55`) and srcdoc iframes stop loading. Code that depends on it: `nsContentSecurityManager.cpp:1821-1826`, `ClientValidation.cpp:102-104`, `ThirdPartyUtil.cpp:191` and `331`, `ReferrerInfo.cpp:281`.
- **Network and data:** none of its own. Whatever the embedding page puts in `srcdoc` loads under that page's rules.
- **Gorilla change:** none. Register: `verdict: keep`, `network: none`. Classed ESSENTIAL.
